## Airport Lighting Calculations: Voltage Drop, Load, Power and Cable Size

Airfield lighting runs on constant-current series circuits: a constant current regulator (CCR) pushes the same
current through every fixture, and the voltage it must deliver depends on the total resistance and impedance
of the loop. The calculators above follow that logic, so you can size a CCR, check a cable run or plan a new
circuit without a spreadsheet.

### Ohms law calculator for AGL circuits

Everything starts with V = I × R . In a series circuit the current is fixed by the CCR brightness step, so the
voltage the CCR must supply is that current multiplied by the total circuit resistance. Power lost as heat in
the cable is P = I² × R . Use the Ohm's Law Calculator to solve any one of V, I, R or P from two known values;
the Series Circuit Impedance , Primary Cable Resistance and Circuit Voltage calculators apply it directly to
airfield circuits.

### Airport lighting series circuit calculator

The Series Circuit Load calculator totals fixture wattage, isolating transformer losses and cable I²R loss,
then checks the result against the CCR. Use AGL Circuit Length Estimator to estimate primary cable from
fixture count and spacing, and Circuit Power Factor when the load mixes fixture types.

### Airport lighting voltage drop calculator, runway lighting voltage drop calculator and taxiway lighting voltage drop calculator

Voltage drop in the primary cable is the circuit current times the cable resistance over its length. A longer
run or a smaller conductor raises it, and the CCR has to make up the difference. The Cable Voltage Drop
calculator handles runway lighting voltage drop, taxiway lighting voltage drop and any other primary series
run, and shows the maximum length for a chosen drop limit. For the short lead between an isolating transformer
and its fixture, use Secondary Cable Voltage Drop .

### Airport lighting cable size calculator

Cable size is chosen so that voltage drop, I²R loss and the cable's voltage rating all stay within limits for
the length of the circuit. Use the AGL Cable Size Selection Calculator to pick the smallest conductor that
meets your limits, or compare conductors in the Cable Voltage Drop , Primary Cable Resistance and Cable Power
Loss calculators.

### Airport lighting load calculation, power calculation and current calculation (load calculator)

An airport lighting load calculation, airport lighting power calculation and airport lighting current
calculation all start from the same circuit data. Circuit load is the sum of all fixture watts, plus isolating
transformer losses and cable loss, expressed in kW and kVA. Current is set by the CCR step you run the circuit
on, so a current calculation is really a check that each step stays within the allowable range; the CCR Step
Current / Brightness Reference lists those steps. To see how many more fixtures an existing circuit can take,
use AGL Spare Capacity Calculator .

### Runway lighting load calculation, runway lighting power calculation, taxiway lighting load calculation and taxiway lighting power calculation

Runway lighting load calculation, runway lighting power calculation, taxiway lighting load calculation and
taxiway lighting power calculation all use the same method as above; only the fixture counts and cable lengths
differ.

### Airport lighting load calculator, runway lighting load calculator, runway lighting power calculator, taxiway lighting load calculator and taxiway lighting power calculator

The Runway & Taxiway Lighting Load / Power Calculator gives kW and kVA by circuit for the runway, the taxiway
and the whole system. The Series Circuit Load calculator works as an airport lighting load calculator, runway
lighting load calculator, runway lighting power calculator, taxiway lighting load calculator and taxiway
lighting power calculator. Enter the fixture count, transformer losses and cable length for the circuit in
question.

### CCR size calculator: kVA calculator for CCR sizing

CCR size is the output voltage times the circuit current, divided by 1,000 to give kVA. The CCR Capacity
calculator adds an expansion allowance and a maximum loading limit, then picks the smallest standard CCR size
that covers the load. CCR Selection & Loading picks the smallest standard CCR and checks loading at every
brightness step. Transformer VA Selection does the equivalent for isolating transformers.

### Energy calculator for airfield lighting

Energy use is power times operating hours, and cost is energy times your tariff. The Cable Power Loss
calculator already reports yearly cable-loss energy. The Series Circuit Energy & Operating Cost calculator
covers CCR load, operating hours and tariff for the full yearly energy and cost.

### Light spacing: approach, runway threshold and stop bar

Light spacing depends on the lighting type and the standard you design to (ICAO Annex 14 or FAA AC
150/5340-30). Try Approach Lighting Quantity Tool for approach light spacing and station counts, Threshold &
Runway-End Lights for runway threshold light spacing, and Stop Bar & Holding Position Lights for stop bar
light spacing. Edge Light Spacing covers runway edge lights.

## AGL Calculations and Light Spacing Reference

### AGL design calculations

AGL design calculations turn a lighting layout into circuit data: number of lights, circuit load, cable
resistance, voltage drop and CCR size. Do them in order, and recheck them when the layout changes. The
calculators above cover each step.

### AGL engineering calculations

AGL engineering calculations cover the electrical sizing of the series circuit and the layout of the lights.
Keep a record of the inputs, the method and the results, so the design can be reviewed and later changes can
be checked.

### Airfield ground lighting calculation

An airfield ground lighting calculation starts with the lights on a circuit and ends with the CCR rating.
Typical steps are fixture and transformer load, cable resistance, total voltage, kVA and a margin for growth.

### Airfield lighting calculation

An airfield lighting calculation sizes the electrical system that feeds the lights: load, current, voltage,
cable and regulator. It is separate from the photometric calculation, which checks the light output.

### Airport lighting calculation

An airport lighting calculation covers the electrical and layout figures behind an AGL design. The sections
below list the main ones, and the calculators above carry them out.

### Runway lighting calculation

A runway lighting calculation finds the number of lights, the circuit split, the load on each circuit and the
size of each CCR. Runway circuits are usually separated so one fault does not remove all the lights.

### Taxiway lighting calculation

A taxiway lighting calculation sizes the circuits for edge and centreline lights, which are often spread over
long and branching routes. Cable length and voltage drop usually need most attention.

### Approach lighting calculation

An approach lighting calculation sizes the circuits for the approach lights, which can be long and carry high-
wattage lamps. Load and cable resistance determine the CCR size and the circuit split.

### Runway edge lights calculation

A runway edge lights calculation counts the lights along both edges and finds the load they place on the
circuit, including the isolating transformers and cable.

### Runway centreline lights calculation

A runway centreline lights calculation counts the lights along the centreline and finds their load on the
circuit. The centreline lights are normally on their own circuit.

### Threshold lights calculation

A threshold lights calculation counts the threshold and wing bar lights and finds their load. They are often
supplied from a separate circuit from the edge lights.

### Airfield lighting load calculation

An airfield lighting load calculation adds the fixture wattages, transformer losses and cable loss to give the
circuit load in kW and kVA. Compare it with the CCR rating and leave spare capacity. The Series Circuit Load
calculator does this.

### AGL power calculation

An AGL power calculation finds the real power and the apparent power drawn by a circuit. The cable loss is I²
× R, and the CCR also has its own losses and power factor, which the manufacturer gives.

### AGL series circuit calculation

An AGL series circuit calculation finds the total resistance or impedance the CCR must drive at full current,
then the voltage and kVA needed. The same current flows through every light.

### Constant current regulator calculation

A constant current regulator calculation finds the output voltage and kVA needed for a circuit, then selects
the next standard CCR size with margin. See CCR Capacity .

### Airfield lighting isolation transformer calculation

An airfield lighting isolation transformer calculation chooses the transformer rating for the lamp wattage,
and adds the transformer losses and magnetising effect to the circuit load. Use the manufacturer's data for
the figures.

### Airfield lighting control system calculation

An airfield lighting control system calculation sizes the control hardware: the number of inputs and outputs,
the circuits to be monitored and the power for the control equipment. It follows the circuit schedule.

### ALCMS calculation

An ALCMS calculation sizes the control and monitoring system: the number of circuits, monitoring points,
panels and communication links. It follows the circuit schedule and the control philosophy.

### Airfield lighting cable calculation

An airfield lighting cable calculation picks a conductor size and checks resistance, voltage drop, I² × R loss
and ratings over the full circuit length. The Cable Voltage Drop calculator supports it.

### AGL cable voltage drop

AGL cable voltage drop is the voltage lost in the cable at the circuit current, I × R. In a series circuit it
adds to the voltage the CCR must supply, so long cables raise the CCR size. Use the Cable Voltage Drop
calculator.

### AGL voltage drop calculation

An AGL voltage drop calculation multiplies the circuit current by the total cable resistance, using the
conductor resistance per length and the full length. Check the result against the CCR output and the cable
rating. See Cable Voltage Drop .

### Runway lights spacing

Runway lights spacing is set by the applicable standard and the approved design, and it depends on the light
type and the layout. The count of lights follows from the length and the spacing, with allowance for ends,
intersections and curves.

### Runway lighting spacing

Runway lighting spacing is set by the applicable standard and the approved design, and it depends on the light
type and the layout. The count of lights follows from the length and the spacing, with allowance for ends,
intersections and curves.

### Runway centreline light spacing

Runway centreline light spacing is set by the applicable standard and the approved design, and it depends on
the light type and the layout. The count of lights follows from the length and the spacing, with allowance for
ends, intersections and curves. The centreline lights are checked against the runway length and any changes in
spacing along it.

### Runway centreline lights spacing

Runway centreline lights spacing is set by the applicable standard and the approved design, and it depends on
the light type and the layout. The count of lights follows from the length and the spacing, with allowance for
ends, intersections and curves.

### Taxiway lighting spacing

Taxiway lighting spacing is set by the applicable standard and the approved design, and it depends on the
light type and the layout. The count of lights follows from the length and the spacing, with allowance for
ends, intersections and curves. Spacing is often closer on curves and at intersections.

### Airfield lighting spacing

Airfield lighting spacing is set by the applicable standard and the approved design, and it depends on the
light type and the layout. The count of lights follows from the length and the spacing, with allowance for
ends, intersections and curves.

### Airfield ground lighting spacing

Airfield ground lighting spacing is set by the applicable standard and the approved design, and it depends on
the light type and the layout. The count of lights follows from the length and the spacing, with allowance for
ends, intersections and curves.

### Airport lighting spacing

Airport lighting spacing is set by the applicable standard and the approved design, and it depends on the
light type and the layout. The count of lights follows from the length and the spacing, with allowance for
ends, intersections and curves.

### Runway light spacing calculation

Runway light spacing calculation is set by the applicable standard and the approved design, and it depends on
the light type and the layout. The count of lights follows from the length and the spacing, with allowance for
ends, intersections and curves. Divide the length by the spacing, then add the end light.

### Taxiway light spacing calculation

Taxiway light spacing calculation is set by the applicable standard and the approved design, and it depends on
the light type and the layout. The count of lights follows from the length and the spacing, with allowance for
ends, intersections and curves.

### Airfield lighting spacing calculation

Airfield lighting spacing calculation is set by the applicable standard and the approved design, and it
depends on the light type and the layout. The count of lights follows from the length and the spacing, with
allowance for ends, intersections and curves.

### AGL series circuit spacing

AGL series circuit spacing is how the lights and transformers are placed along a circuit. Placement sets the
cable length, so it affects the circuit resistance and voltage drop.

### Constant current regulator spacing

Constant current regulator spacing is where the CCRs are placed in relation to the circuits they feed. A CCR
close to its circuit reduces the cable length and the voltage drop.

### Airfield lighting isolation transformer spacing

Airfield lighting isolation transformer spacing follows the light spacing, as there is normally one
transformer for each light. Place it close to the fixture so the secondary leads stay short.

### Airfield lighting cable spacing

Airfield lighting cable spacing covers the separation between cables, ducts and other services. It affects
heating, installation and fault risk, and comes from the cable data and the design.

### Airfield lighting control system spacing

Airfield lighting control system spacing is how control and monitoring equipment is spread over the airfield.
It follows the circuit layout and the communication limits of the equipment.

### ALCMS spacing

ALCMS spacing is where the ALCMS field units, panels and network nodes are placed. It follows the circuit
layout, the cable routes and the communication limits.

## AGL Calculation Questions

### How is airport lighting load calculated?

Add the wattage of every fixture on the circuit, then add the losses in the isolating transformers and the I²R
loss in the primary cable. The total, in kW and kVA, is the circuit load. Compare it with the CCR rating,
leaving spare capacity for expansion. The Series Circuit Load calculator does this.

### How is CCR size calculated?

Work out the voltage the CCR must supply at full current (current times total circuit resistance or
impedance), multiply by that current to get kVA, add an allowance for growth, and choose the next standard
size up. See CCR Capacity .

### How is airport lighting cable sized?

Pick a conductor whose resistance keeps voltage drop and I²R loss acceptable over the full circuit length, and
whose voltage and current ratings suit the circuit. Larger conductors lower the loss but cost more, so
designers compare options. The Cable Voltage Drop and Primary Cable Resistance calculators support that
comparison.

### How is airport lighting voltage drop calculated?

Multiply the circuit current by the resistance of the cable section (resistance per unit length times length,
corrected for temperature). Sum the sections for the whole run. The Cable Voltage Drop calculator works
section by section.

### How to calculate AGL voltage drop?

Multiply the circuit current by the total cable resistance, which is the conductor resistance per length times
the full circuit length. In a series circuit the current is set by the CCR brightness step, and the voltage
drop adds to the voltage the CCR must supply. Check the result against the CCR output and the cable rating
with the Cable Voltage Drop calculator.

### How to calculate runway light spacing?

Take the required spacing for the light type from the applicable standard and the approved design, then divide
the length to be lit by that spacing and add the end light. Adjust for intersections, curves and changes in
spacing, and round to whole lights. The light count then feeds the load and CCR calculations.

### AGL Topic Hub: Search 800+ Airfield Ground Lighting Topics

Canonical URL: https://rahulsharmaagl.in/topic-hub.html

**Page summary:** Search 800+ airfield ground lighting topics: AGL components, ICAO & FAA standards, SOPs, troubleshooting, case studies and comparisons in one hub.

# Topic Hub

Search across every component, standard, diagram topic, and glossary term in the AGL Knowledge Hub — one index
connecting the entire platform.

#### Runway Edge Light

Defines the lateral limits of the runway for night and low-visibility operations. Emits white light except on
the last 600m where it shifts to amber/yellow.

#### Elevated Runway Edge Light

A raised fixture mounted on frangible poles above ground level, providing runway edge delineation with
improved visibility in snow or uneven terrain.

#### Inset Runway Edge Light

A flush-mounted fixture set into the pavement surface, providing runway edge delineation on paved runways
where elevated fixtures would interfere with snowplows or aircraft.

#### Runway Centreline Light

Flush-mounted lights along the runway centreline spaced at 15m or 30m intervals, providing guidance during
take-off and landing roll.

#### Runway Threshold Light

Green lights marking the beginning of the runway available for landing, arranged in a bar across the
threshold, visible only from the approach side.

#### Runway End Light

Red lights marking the end of the runway available for landing, visible only from the approach side,
indicating the runway boundary.

#### Threshold Wing Bar Light

A row of green lights extending outward from the runway threshold, forming a wing bar pattern to clearly
identify the landing threshold.

#### Wing Bar Light

A row of lights perpendicular to the runway centreline, typically green for threshold wing bars, enhancing
visual identification of the runway end.

#### Touchdown Zone Light (TDZ)

Flush-mounted lights in the first 900m of the runway from the threshold, spaced at 30m intervals, identifying
the touchdown zone for precision approaches.

#### Runway End Identifier Light (REIL)

A pair of synchronized flashing lights, one on each side of the runway threshold, helping pilots identify the
runway end during approach.

#### Runway Guard Light

A pair of flashing amber lights installed at runway holding positions, warning pilots and vehicle drivers that
they are approaching an active runway.

#### Runway Status Light (RWSL)

An automated system of in-pavement lights that provides direct visual indication of runway occupancy and
clearance status to pilots.

#### Take-Off Hold Light (THL)

Red lights embedded in the runway surface at the take-off hold position, indicating to pilots that the runway
is not clear for take-off.

#### Runway Entrance Light (REL)

A line of red lights embedded in the runway surface at the runway entrance, indicating that the runway is
occupied by another aircraft.

#### Final Approach Runway Occupancy Signal (FAROS)

A visual warning system that alerts landing pilots when the runway is occupied, using flashing red approach
lights.

#### Lead-on Light

A sequence of lights guiding an aircraft from the taxiway onto the runway centreline, typically flashing in
sequence to indicate direction.

#### Lead-off Light

A sequence of lights guiding an aircraft from the runway centreline onto an exit taxiway, typically flashing
in sequence to indicate direction.

#### Rapid Exit Taxiway Indicator

A row of lights on the runway indicating the location of a rapid exit taxiway, helping pilots identify turn-
off points during landing roll.

#### Green Threshold Light

A green light fixture at the runway threshold, part of the threshold bar, indicating the start of the runway
landing area.

#### Red Runway End Light

A red light fixture at the runway end, part of the end bar, indicating the end of the runway available for
landing.

#### Combination Threshold/End Light

A bi-color fixture that displays green from the approach side and red from the opposite side, serving as both
threshold and end light.

#### Omnidirectional Runway Edge Light

A runway edge light that emits light uniformly in all directions, visible from any angle, typically used on
non-precision runways.

#### High Intensity Runway Light

A runway edge light with high luminous intensity, typically rated at 10,000 cd or more, suitable for CAT
II/III precision approach runways.

#### Medium Intensity Runway Light

A runway edge light with medium luminous intensity, typically rated at 2,000–5,000 cd, suitable for CAT I or
non-precision runways.

#### Low Intensity Runway Light

A runway edge light with low luminous intensity, typically rated below 1,000 cd, suitable for non-instrument
or visual runways.

#### High-Intensity Runway Centreline Light

An AGL fixture along the centreline of the high-intensity runway centreline, providing precise guidance for
aircraft during ground movement or take-off/landing roll.

#### Bidirectional Runway Centreline Light

An AGL fixture along the centreline of the bidirectional runway centreline, providing precise guidance for
aircraft during ground movement or take-off/landing roll.

#### Unidirectional Runway Centreline Light

An AGL fixture along the centreline of the unidirectional runway centreline, providing precise guidance for
aircraft during ground movement or take-off/landing roll.

#### Unidirectional Touchdown Zone Light

An AGL fixture providing visual guidance for aircraft operations, with specific photometric characteristics
for its intended application.

#### Bidirectional/Omnidirectional Runway Edge Fixture

A critical AGL component that provides essential functionality for airfield ground lighting operations,
supporting safe aircraft movements in all visibility conditions.

#### Runway Exit Light

An AGL fixture providing visual guidance for aircraft operations, with specific photometric characteristics
for its intended application.

#### Taxiway Edge Light

Blue lights outlining the edges of taxiways, providing guidance for aircraft during ground movement in low
visibility.

#### Taxiway Centreline Light

Green lights along the taxiway centreline, providing guidance during ground movement, especially in low
visibility conditions.

#### Elevated Taxiway Light

A raised fixture on a frangible pole, providing taxiway edge or centreline guidance, often used where snow or
terrain makes flush mounting impractical.

#### Inset Taxiway Light

A flush-mounted taxiway light set into the pavement, providing edge or centreline guidance without protruding
above the surface.

#### Taxiway Curve Light

A series of lights marking a curve or turn on a taxiway, typically with closer spacing than straight sections
to guide pilots through the turn.

#### Rapid Exit Taxiway Centreline Light

A line of green lights leading from the runway centreline to a rapid exit taxiway, showing pilots where to
turn off after landing.

#### Intermediate Holding Position Light

Yellow lights at an intermediate holding position on a taxiway, indicating where aircraft must stop and await
clearance.

#### Stop Bar Light

A row of red lights across a taxiway at a runway holding position, indicating that aircraft must stop and
hold.

#### Clearance Bar Light

A row of lights across a taxiway at a runway holding position, used in conjunction with stop bars to provide
clearance indication.

#### Taxiway Lead-on Light

A sequence of green lights guiding an aircraft from a taxiway onto the runway centreline, flashing in sequence
to indicate direction.

#### Taxiway Lead-off Light

A sequence of green lights guiding an aircraft from the runway centreline onto an exit taxiway, flashing in
sequence to indicate direction.

#### Apron Taxiway Light

Lights on the apron or ramp area, typically blue or green, guiding aircraft to and from parking positions and
gates.

#### Taxi Guidance Light

A light system providing direction guidance on taxiways, often using a combination of edge and centreline
lights with specific color coding.

#### Apron Flood Light

High-intensity floodlights mounted on tall masts, providing general illumination of the apron area for
aircraft parking and servicing.

#### Blue Edge Light

A blue light indicating the edge of a taxiway or apron area, helping pilots maintain position during ground
movement.

#### Green Centreline Light

A green light on the taxiway centreline, providing guidance during ground movement, especially in low
visibility.

#### Yellow Clearance Bar

A yellow light bar across a taxiway indicating a holding position where clearance from ATC is required.

#### Taxiway Intersection Light

An AGL fixture providing visual guidance for aircraft operations, with specific photometric characteristics
for its intended application.

#### Taxiway Runway Turnoff Light

An AGL fixture providing visual guidance for aircraft operations, with specific photometric characteristics
for its intended application.

#### Taxiway Turnoff/Runway Exit Indicator Fixture

A critical AGL component that provides essential functionality for airfield ground lighting operations,
supporting safe aircraft movements in all visibility conditions.

#### Intermediate Holding Position Fixture

A critical AGL component that provides essential functionality for airfield ground lighting operations,
supporting safe aircraft movements in all visibility conditions.

#### Stop Bar Monitoring Unit

An AGL unit used in airfield ground lighting systems for stop bar monitoring unit.

#### Stop Bar Control Module

A modular electronic component for AGL systems, providing specific functionality such as control, regulation,
or communication.

#### Stop Bar Inset Fixture

A critical AGL component that provides essential functionality for airfield ground lighting operations,
supporting safe aircraft movements in all visibility conditions.

#### Elevated Stop Bar Fixture

A critical AGL component that provides essential functionality for airfield ground lighting operations,
supporting safe aircraft movements in all visibility conditions.

#### Taxiway Centreline Alternate-Circuit Fixture

A critical AGL component that provides essential functionality for airfield ground lighting operations,
supporting safe aircraft movements in all visibility conditions.

#### Taxiway Edge Omni Fixture

A critical AGL component that provides essential functionality for airfield ground lighting operations,
supporting safe aircraft movements in all visibility conditions.

#### ALSF-1

Approach Lighting System with Sequenced Flashing lights — a CAT I precision approach lighting system with a
720m long configuration, including barrettes and sequenced flashing lights.

#### ALSF-2

Approach Lighting System with Sequenced Flashing lights — a CAT II/III precision approach lighting system with
a 900m long configuration, providing enhanced visual guidance for low-visibility approaches.

#### CAT I Approach Lighting

Approach lighting system for Category I precision approaches, typically consisting of a 720m or 900m
configuration with barrettes and flashing lights.

#### CAT II Approach Lighting

Approach lighting system for Category II precision approaches, featuring enhanced configuration with
additional barrettes and centerline lights for 350m RVR.

#### CAT III Approach Lighting

Approach lighting system for Category III precision approaches, featuring full 900m configuration with high-
intensity lights for 200m or lower RVR.

#### Simple Approach Lighting System (SALS)

A basic approach lighting system consisting of a single row of lights extending from the runway threshold,
used on non-precision runways.

#### SSALS

Simplified Short Approach Lighting System — a shorter configuration of approach lights for non-precision
runways, typically 420m in length.

#### MALS

Medium Intensity Approach Lighting System — a moderate-intensity system for non-precision runways, providing
approach guidance with fewer lights than ALSF.

#### MALSF

Medium Intensity Approach Lighting System with Sequenced Flashing lights — an approach lighting system with
flashing lights for enhanced visual guidance.

#### MALSR

Medium Intensity Approach Lighting System with Runway Alignment Indicator Lights — an approach lighting system
with sequenced flashing lights for runway alignment.

#### ODALS

Omnidirectional Approach Lighting System — a system of omnidirectional lights providing approach guidance,
often used at smaller airfields.

#### Calvert System

A British-developed approach lighting system featuring a distinctive "barrette" pattern of lights, designed to
provide both horizontal and vertical guidance.

#### Sequenced Flashing Lights

A row of lights that flash in sequence from the outer end toward the runway threshold, providing a visual
"rolling" effect that indicates approach direction.

#### Flashing Approach Lights

A series of lights that flash in sequence, typically white, providing enhanced visual guidance during
approach, especially in low visibility.

#### Crossbar Lights

A row of lights perpendicular to the approach path, typically at fixed distances from the threshold, providing
lateral guidance and distance reference.

#### Side Row Bars

Rows of lights on either side of the approach centerline, providing lateral guidance and defining the approach
corridor.

#### Decision Bar

A row of lights at the decision height point on the approach, providing a visual reference for the pilot's
go/no-go decision.

#### Centreline Barrette

A short row of lights on the approach centerline, typically 1m apart, providing precise lateral guidance
during approach.

#### Lead-in Lighting

A series of lights guiding aircraft from the approach path to the runway threshold, typically used at airports

#### PAPI

#### VASI

beam direction.

#### Test Bench

A workbench and testing station for AGL fixture testing and maintenance, typically equipped with power
supplies, meters, and optical equipment.

#### Lux Meter

A handheld instrument that measures illuminance in lux, used for checking lighting levels and uniformity on
the airfield.

#### Digital Level

A digital inclinometer used for checking the level and orientation of AGL fixtures, ensuring proper beam angle
and alignment.

#### GPS Receiver

A GPS receiver for measuring fixture positions and verifying installation coordinates, ensuring accurate
placement of AGL components.

#### Lamp Extractor

A tool used for removing lamps from AGL fixtures, providing safe and efficient lamp replacement without
damaging the fixture.

#### Fixture Lifting Tool

A tool for lifting and handling AGL fixtures during installation and maintenance, preventing damage and
ensuring safety.

#### Torque Wrench

A wrench with torque measurement, used for tightening fasteners to specified torque values during AGL fixture
installation.

#### Prism Cleaning Kit

A kit containing cleaning materials and solutions for cleaning prisms and lenses of AGL fixtures, maintaining
optical clarity.

#### Cable Tester

A device for testing cable continuity, insulation resistance, and other parameters of AGL cables, verifying
cable integrity.

#### Insulation Resistance Tester

A device for measuring insulation resistance of AGL cables and transformers, ensuring electrical safety and
detecting faults.

#### HV Tester

A high-voltage tester for checking the dielectric strength of AGL cables and equipment, ensuring insulation
integrity.

#### Transformer Tester

A test instrument for checking transformer parameters, including turns ratio, inductance, and resistance,
verifying transformer health.

#### Loop Resistance Meter

A meter for measuring the resistance of the series lighting loop, checking circuit continuity and detecting
faults.

#### Clamp Meter

A clamp-on meter for measuring current without breaking the circuit, used for AGL loop current measurement and
troubleshooting.

#### Multimeter

A general-purpose electrical meter for measuring voltage, current, resistance, and other parameters, used for
AGL system troubleshooting.

#### Earth Tester

A tester for measuring earth resistance of earthing systems, verifying the integrity of earthing connections
for AGL equipment.

#### Runway

A paved strip on an airport used for aircraft take-off and landing, typically with AGL lighting systems for
night and low-visibility operations.

#### Taxiway

A paved path on an airport used for aircraft ground movement between the runway and apron, typically with AGL
lighting for guidance.

#### Apron

A paved area on an airport used for aircraft parking, loading, and servicing, typically with floodlighting and
taxi guidance lights.

#### Holding Bay

A designated area where aircraft can hold on the taxiway, typically with holding position lights and signs for
guidance.

#### Blast Pad

A paved area at the runway ends that resists jet blast, providing protection from engine exhaust and
preventing surface erosion.

#### Stopway

A paved area beyond the runway end that can support an aircraft that overruns the runway, providing
deceleration capability.

#### RESA

Runway End Safety Area — a cleared area beyond the runway end providing a buffer zone for aircraft that
overrun or undershoot the runway.

#### Shoulder

A paved or stabilized strip adjacent to the runway or taxiway, providing support for the pavement edge and
equipment access.

#### Service Road

A road on the airfield used for vehicle access to AGL equipment and airfield facilities, separate from
aircraft movement areas.

#### Equipment Shelter

A shelter that houses AGL equipment such as CCRs, transformers, and control panels, protecting them from
environmental damage.

#### Visual Docking Guidance System (VDGS)

A system that provides pilots with real-time visual guidance to safely park aircraft at the stand, typically
displaying azimuth, lateral deviation, distance to stop, and stop position using laser, radar, or camera
sensors. It enhances apron safety and turnaround efficiency.

#### LED PCB

A printed circuit board containing LED chips and drive circuits, providing electrical and thermal management
for LED-based AGL fixtures.

#### Constant Current Module

A module that provides constant current regulation for LED fixtures, ensuring stable light output regardless
of input voltage variations.

#### Surge Module

A module that provides surge protection for LED AGL fixtures, protecting sensitive electronics from lightning
and transient voltage spikes.

#### EMI Filter

An electromagnetic interference filter for LED AGL fixtures, reducing conducted emissions and ensuring
compliance with EMC standards.

#### Thermal Pad

A thermally conductive pad placed between the LED module and heat sink, providing efficient heat transfer for
proper thermal management.

#### Heat Pipe

A heat transfer device that efficiently conducts heat away from the LED light source, enabling high-power LED
operation in AGL fixtures.

#### IoT Gateway

An Internet of Things gateway that connects smart AGL devices to the cloud, enabling remote monitoring,
control, and data analytics.

#### Wireless Sensor

A wireless sensor for AGL monitoring, typically using LoRa or ZigBee for communication, providing data on
fixture status, temperature, and current.

#### Smart Fixture

An AGL fixture with embedded electronics and communication capability, providing status monitoring, fault
detection, and remote control.

#### Smart Transformer

An isolating transformer with embedded sensing and communication, providing status monitoring and fault
detection for AGL series circuits.

#### Cloud Gateway

A gateway that connects AGL systems to cloud-based monitoring and analytics platforms, enabling predictive
maintenance and remote diagnostics.

#### Remote Diagnostics Module

A module that enables remote diagnostics of AGL equipment, providing fault detection, troubleshooting support,
and performance monitoring.

#### Predictive Maintenance Sensor

A sensor that monitors AGL equipment health and predicts maintenance needs, using data analytics to optimize
maintenance schedules.

#### DGCA CAR Section 4, Series B, Part I — Aerodrome Design & Operations

India's actual controlling aerodrome design requirement — substantially adopts ICAO Annex 14, Volume I as
binding domestic law.

#### ICAO Annex 14 — Edge Light Spacing

Maximum 60m spacing requirement for runway edge lights.

#### ICAO Annex 14 — Edge Light Colour

Variable white with yellow caution zone requirements.

Constant current regulator output regulation tolerance.

#### FAA AC 150/5345-47 — Transformer Insulation

Hi-pot testing requirements for isolating transformers.

#### IEC 61822 — Series Circuit Testing

Fault condition testing for series AGL equipment.

#### IEC 61820-3-2:2023 — Power Supplies for AGL Series Circuits

Current IEC standard for power electronic converter systems (PECS), including 6.6A CCR setups, powering AGL
series circuits. Replaces IEC 61822:2009.

#### IEC 61820/61821/61823/62144 — AGL Electrical Series Family

Map of the wider IEC 618xx family — system design, maintenance, series transformers, and control/monitoring
beyond the CCR-focused standards.

#### ICAO Annex 14 — PAPI Siting

Obstacle clearance requirements for PAPI glide path calculation.

#### FAA AC 150/5340-30J — Design & Installation Details for Airport Visual Aids

Consolidated FAA installation-detail AC covering edge/centerline/TDZ lighting, approach lighting, PAPI, signs,
and wind cones.

#### ICAO Annex 14 — Runway Threshold & Wing Bar Lights

Green, one-way lights mark exactly where the usable runway begins — and must move with the threshold if it's
ever displaced.

#### ICAO Annex 14 — Runway End Lights

Red, one-way lights mark the far end of the runway for an aircraft already on it — the mirror image of the
green threshold lights.

#### ICAO Annex 14 — Runway Centreline Lights Requirements

Runway centreline lights requirements: colour shifts from white toward red as the runway end approaches,
giving a pilot a built-in countdown on CAT II/III approaches.

#### ICAO Annex 14 — Touchdown Zone Lights

White barrettes run 900m from the threshold or to the runway midpoint — whichever is shorter, so short runways
get proportionally less coverage.

#### ICAO Annex 14 — Taxiway Centre Line Lights

Green inset lights that pull in tighter on curves and change treatment specifically where they cross a runway.

#### ICAO Annex 14 — Taxiway Edge Lights

Blue elevated lights mark the lateral limits of a taxiway — the one colour in the AGL palette reserved
exclusively for this job.

#### ICAO Annex 14 — Stop Bars

Red lights across the taxiway that must never be lit at the same moment as the centre line lights beyond them
— the interlock is safety-critical.

#### ICAO Annex 14 — Runway Guard Lights

Yellow flashing lights at the holding position — a visual warning cue, not a physical interlock like a stop
bar.

#### IS 12290:1987 — Isolating Transformers for Airport Lighting

India's core specification for series isolating transformers — construction, ratings, and insulation
resistance.

#### FAA AC 150/5345-26E — L-823 Plug & Receptacle Cable Connectors

Covers L-823 plug/receptacle connectors for underground power cable, transformer leads, and fixture leads.

#### FAA AC 150/5345-7F — L-824 Underground Electrical Cable

Specifies L-824 series-circuit cable — 5,000V, non-shielded, single-conductor 7-strand — with production
testing.

#### FAA AC 150/5345-28H — L-880/L-881 PAPI Systems

Covers L-880 (4-unit) and L-881 (2-unit) PAPI light housings — remote control and selectable night-mode
intensity.

#### FAA AC 150/5345-46F — Runway, Taxiway, Heliport & Vertiport Light Fixtures

Current FAA fixture spec, extended to cover heliport and vertiport fixtures alongside runway/taxiway types.

#### FAA AC 150/5345-42K — Light Bases, Transformer Housings & Junction Boxes

#### FAA AC 150/5345-44 — Runway & Taxiway Signs

Covers the six FAA sign types, in five sizes and five styles, used on runways and taxiways.

#### ICAO Annex 14 — Obstacle Lighting

Object height and background decide low/medium/high-intensity class — steady red for night, flashing white for
daytime conspicuity.

#### ICAO Annex 14 — Approach Lighting Systems (ALS)

Light-bar length and configuration scale directly with the runway's approach category, from a simple SALS up

#### FAA AC 150/5345-53D — Airport Lighting Equipment Certification Program

#### IEC 61821:2011 — Maintenance of Aeronautical Ground Lighting

#### ICAO Annex 14 — Aerodrome Beacon

Alternating white/green flashes mark the aerodrome's location for aircraft in flight — a location aid, not a
runway cue.

#### FAA AC 150/5345-43 — Obstruction Lighting Equipment

Covers low- (L-810), medium- (L-864/L-865) and high-intensity (L-856) obstruction light equipment for

#### ICAO Annex 14 — Mandatory Instruction & Guidance Signs

Red background with white legend means stop-and-clear; the complementary yellow/black scheme is wayfinding
only.

#### ICAO Annex 14 — Illuminated Wind Direction Indicator

Sited for unobstructed airflow from every likely wind direction, not just the prevailing one — illuminated for
night operations.

#### IEC 61823 — Aeronautical Beacons

#### FAA AC 150/5345-56B — L-890 Airport Lighting Control & Monitoring System (ALCMS)

PLC-based system centralizing AGL switching and status monitoring, across four escalating monitoring tiers.

#### FAA AC 150/5345-3G — L-821 Panels for the Control of Airport Lighting

Covers the L-847 switch used to route a single CCR's output across one or more series lighting circuits.

## Frequently Asked Questions

Quick answers about the AGL SOP Library and how its 22 divisions are organized.

The AGL SOP Library by Precision AGL Academy is a collection of 480 Standard Operating Procedures for airfield
ground lighting, organized into 22 divisions. It covers testing, maintenance and field operations, drawn from
real airport project experience. All 22 divisions are published (Rev 0, initial issue).

By division, each with its own SOP number range. Divisions 01–02 cover airside safety and electrical
safety/LOTO; 03–07 cover planning, civil works, cabling and isolation transformers; 08–12 cover runway,
taxiway and approach lighting, PAPI/VASI and signage; and 13–15 cover CCR and series circuits, ALCMS and
earthing. Divisions 16–19 cover inspection, testing and photometry, maintenance and commissioning, and 20–22
cover emergency response, documentation and training.

Division 02 — Electrical Safety, LOTO & Isolation (SOP-26 → SOP-50, 25 procedures). Airside work permits and
runway or taxiway proximity rules are in Division 01 — Airside Safety & Work Permit (SOP-01 → SOP-25, 25
procedures).

Runway Lighting is Division 08, Taxiway Lighting Division 09, Approach Lighting Division 10, PAPI / VASI
Division 11 and Airfield Signage Division 12. Inspection, testing and maintenance of these systems are covered
in Divisions 16, 17 and 18.

CCR & Series Circuit is Division 13 (25 procedures), ALCMS / Control & Monitoring is Division 14 (20
procedures) and Earthing, Bonding & Lightning Protection is Division 15 (20 procedures).

Commissioning & Acceptance is Division 19, Emergency Response is Division 20 and Documentation, Records &
Reporting is Division 21. Training, Competency & Knowledge Management is Division 22.

No. The SOPs are a technical framework. Each division states that approved project drawings, manufacturer's
instructions, applicable standards and the airport's own procedures, permit-to-work system, ATC instructions
and local regulations take precedence, and each airport should adapt them to its own manuals and requirements.

Please read before relying on any content on this page or on any SOP downloaded from it.

- Purpose and intended users. These SOPs are independent educational and reference templates for competent, suitably trained and authorised airfield ground lighting (AGL) and aerodrome electrical personnel. They are not professional engineering, legal, safety or regulatory advice, and using them does not create any professional or client relationship.

- Safety. Work on series circuits, constant current regulators (CCRs), isolating transformers, cables and connectors can be fatal. Always apply the aerodrome’s permit-to-work and isolation/LOTO procedures, prove dead, use correctly rated instruments and PPE, and follow the manufacturer’s instructions. Nothing here authorises work on live equipment or the bypassing of any safety device or interlock.

- Not approved or controlled documents. The SOPs, their numbers and their revision labels are generic templates. They are not approved, issued or controlled documents of any aerodrome, airline, contractor or regulator. Before use, your organisation must review them against its own equipment, hazards and legal duties, adapt them, and approve and issue them under its own document-control and safety management system. Signature blocks and acknowledgement tables on downloaded copies are blank templates and carry no approval or authorisation until completed under that system.

- Aviation operations. Nothing on this page authorises return to service, closure or opening of any aerodrome area, a change of operating category, a NOTAM or any aerodrome certification decision. These rest with the aerodrome operator, the air navigation service provider and the competent regulator. The aerodrome’s approved procedures, permit-to-work system, SMS, ATC instructions and local regulations always take precedence.

- Standards and regulations. References to ICAO, FAA, IEC, IEEE, ISO, DGCA and other documents are summaries for orientation only. They may be incomplete or out of date, and standards are revised from time to time. Consult the current official editions. Following this content does not guarantee compliance with any law, standard or regulatory approval. Official documents, regulations and manufacturers’ instructions always prevail.

- Generic content; no warranty. Steps, sequences, values, tolerances, intervals and criteria are generic and indicative; real installations differ in design, equipment make and model, age and condition. Content is provided “as is” and “as available”, without warranty of any kind, express or implied, including accuracy, completeness, currency or fitness for a particular purpose.

Third-party names, standard designations and trademarks belong to their respective owners and are used for identification only.

compliance.

#### Airfield Signage Troubleshooting

Airfield sign illumination faults, LED/driver failure, water ingress, incorrect installation, and message
display errors.

#### AGL Cable Troubleshooting

Primary/secondary cable open circuits, insulation failure, jointing faults, mechanical damage, and rain/flood-
related faults.

#### L-823 / Connector Troubleshooting

L-823 connector faults — loose connections, burnt contacts, improper crimping, water ingress, and seal
failure.

#### Series Circuit Electrical Faults

Series circuit electrical faults — resistance anomalies, current imbalance, earth faults, and
intermittent/two-point faults.

#### Earthing / Lightning / Surge Troubleshooting

Earthing integrity, lightning damage, surge protection device failure, and ground potential difference
problems.

#### Installation & Commissioning Faults

Installation and commissioning defects — mounting, torque, cable routing, earthing, and commissioning test

#### AGL Photometry Troubleshooting

Photometric faults — low/uneven intensity, beam misalignment, chromaticity error, and measurement/calibration

#### ALCMS / Control & Monitoring

ALCMS faults — communication failure, wrong status/current display, remote command failure, and HMI/data
logging faults.

#### CAT I / CAT II / CAT III Troubleshooting

CAT I/II/III operational lighting failures, low-visibility operation faults, and redundancy/standby system

## Airport Lighting Maintenance, Inspection & Fault Finding

The 30 divisions below hold the detailed fault topics. This guide shows how they fit into day-to-day AGL work:
finding a fault, inspecting the field, keeping to a maintenance schedule and replacing failed lights. Each
block links to the divisions that carry the full diagnostic records.

### Airport Lighting Fault Finding, Fault Diagnosis & Fault Detection

Airport lighting fault finding starts with the symptom and works inward: which lights are out, on which
circuit, at which brightness step. Airport lighting fault diagnosis then narrows that symptom to a section of
the circuit using CCR readings, insulation resistance and continuity checks. Airport lighting fault detection
is what flags the problem in the first place, through ALCMS alarms, CCR output monitoring and field
inspection.

- Emergency quick-diagnosis for a fast first response

- Diagnostic decision trees for step-by-step fault location

- Series circuit electrical faults for earth faults and open circuits

### AGL Fault Testing

AGL fault testing follows a fixed order: confirm the CCR output, check the circuit for earth leakage, then
isolate the faulty section by splitting the loop.

### Airport Lighting Fault Monitoring & the Fault Monitor

Airport lighting fault monitoring relies on the control and monitoring system to report lamp-out counts,
circuit current, earth-fault status and CCR alarms to the tower and maintenance room. An airport lighting
fault monitor is the unit or software function that collects these signals and raises the alarm when a
threshold is crossed.

Monitoring tells you that a fault exists and roughly where. It does not replace a field check, so alarms
should always be confirmed on site.

- ALCMS / control & monitoring

- Difficult / intermittent faults when alarms come and go

### Runway Lighting Common Faults & Runway Lighting Partial Failure

Runway lighting common faults include lamp failure, cracked or flooded fixtures, damaged connectors, isolating
transformer failure, cable insulation breakdown and CCR faults. A runway lighting partial failure means some
lights on a circuit are out while others stay lit, which usually points to individual lamps, transformers or
connectors rather than the CCR.

### What Causes Runway Light Failure?

When people ask what causes runway light failure , the usual answers are moisture ingress, lamp ageing,
connector damage, surge and lightning damage, cable faults and aircraft or vehicle impact. A whole circuit
going dark points to the CCR, the main cable or an open circuit.

### Runway Lighting Troubleshooting Guide

For a complete runway lighting troubleshooting guide , start with the divisions below, which cover each light
type in the runway system.

- Runway edge light troubleshooting

- Runway centreline light troubleshooting

- Touchdown zone light troubleshooting

- Stop bar / guard light troubleshooting

### What Causes Taxiway Light Failure?

The causes of taxiway light failure are similar to runway lights but with more damage from ground vehicles,
aircraft wheel loads and jet blast. Typical causes are water in the fixture, lamp burnout, damaged base can or
connector, failed isolating transformer and cable damage from excavation.

Blue edge lights and green centreline lights can also lose colour or intensity from dirty lenses or a worn
filter, so a light that is on but dim still counts as a fault.

- Taxiway light troubleshooting

- Taxiway centreline / guidance lighting

### Airport Lighting Night & Day Inspection, Periodic Inspection & Inspection Report

An airport lighting night inspection checks what only shows when the lights are on: outages, uneven
brightness, wrong colour, misaligned or obscured lights. An airport lighting day inspection checks the
physical condition: lenses, fixtures, base cans, covers, signs, paint, drainage and vegetation.

The same split applies to specific areas. Runway lighting night inspection and runway lighting day inspection
cover runway edge, threshold, centreline and touchdown lights, and approach lighting night inspection covers
the approach bars and lamps from the air side and, where permitted, from an aircraft or vehicle.

### AGL Periodic Inspection & AGL Inspection Report

AGL periodic inspection covers scheduled checks at set intervals set by the aerodrome operator and regulator.
Each one should end in an AGL inspection report that records date, area, defects found, action taken and who
signed it off.

- Preventive troubleshooting

- Operational & maintenance problems

### AGL Testing, Inspection & Maintenance Checklists

A good checklist keeps the work repeatable between technicians and shifts. The Atlas checklist library is the
place to start. Typical checklist types are:

- AGL testing checklist and airport lighting testing checklist : CCR output, insulation resistance, continuity, earth checks and brightness steps

- Airport lighting inspection checklist : visual condition and lamp status across the airfield

### Runway Lighting Checklist & Taxiway Lighting Checklist

- Runway lighting checklist , with a runway lighting inspection checklist , runway lighting maintenance checklist and runway lighting commissioning checklist for each stage of the equipment life

- Taxiway lighting checklist , with a taxiway lighting inspection checklist , taxiway lighting maintenance checklist and taxiway lighting commissioning checklist

### Approach Lighting Checklist & PAPI Maintenance Checklist

- Approach lighting checklist and approach lighting maintenance checklist

- PAPI maintenance checklist : alignment, lens condition, lamp and heater checks

What is an AGL maintenance checklist? See the answer in the FAQ below.

### Maintenance Types & Schedule: Preventive, Corrective, Emergency & Breakdown

An airport lighting maintenance schedule sets out what is checked daily, weekly, monthly and yearly. Airport
lighting preventive maintenance follows that schedule to catch wear before it causes an outage: cleaning,
torque checks, insulation tests and lamp changes.

Airport lighting corrective maintenance fixes a known defect on a planned job. Airport lighting emergency
maintenance and airport lighting breakdown maintenance deal with failures that affect operations and need an
immediate response, often under a NOTAM or reduced-visibility restrictions.

- Preventive troubleshooting

- Emergency quick-diagnosis

- CAT I / II / III troubleshooting for low-visibility requirements

### Airport Lighting Replacement Procedure

An airport lighting replacement procedure follows the same safe order in every case: get permission and
isolate the circuit, lock out and earth the CCR output, prove it dead, replace the part, test, and restore
with approval from control.

### Runway Light Replacement, Taxiway Light Replacement & Approach Lighting Replacement

- Runway light replacement : match the fixture type, lamp and filter; check the seal, torque and alignment

- Taxiway light replacement : check colour, lens orientation and base can condition

- Approach lighting replacement : replace the fixture or lamp, then check aiming and frangible mounting

- Runway light maintenance procedure : clean, inspect, test and record on every visit, not only when replacing

Never work on a live series circuit. The current in a series loop can stay present even when lights look off.

- Isolating transformer troubleshooting

- L-823 / connector troubleshooting

- Installation & commissioning faults

### AGL Maintenance Technician & Maintenance Training

An airport lighting maintenance technician needs to understand series circuits, CCR operation, high-voltage
safety, test equipment and the aerodrome's operating procedures. AGL maintenance training should cover both
theory and hands-on fault finding, and be kept current as equipment changes.

- Root cause analysis / failure investigation

- Field case study troubleshooting

- Precision AGL Academy training pathway

## Airfield Lighting Troubleshooting & Fault Diagnosis Guide

### AGL electrical fault finding

AGL electrical fault finding starts with the symptom and the circuit, then uses measurements to narrow down
where the fault is. Typical checks are CCR output current, circuit resistance, insulation resistance and
continuity, and they should be done with the circuit isolated and made safe.

### AGL fault alarm system

An AGL fault alarm system reports problems such as an open circuit, an earth fault, a CCR fault or lamps out.
Alarms point to the circuit or unit, but the fault still has to be found and confirmed in the field.

### Airport lighting fault indication

Airport lighting fault indication is the information the CCR and control system give about the state of each
circuit: status, alarms and fault codes. Use it as the starting point and check the field before concluding.

### AGL earth fault

An AGL earth fault is an unwanted path from the circuit to earth, usually from damaged insulation, water in a
connector or transformer, or a damaged cable. It can trip the CCR or leave the circuit running with reduced
protection, so find and repair it promptly.

### Airfield lighting intermittent fault

An airfield lighting intermittent fault comes and goes, often because of moisture, a loose or corroded
connector, a damaged cable or temperature changes. Record when it occurs, look for patterns, and test under
the conditions in which it appears.

### Airfield lighting troubleshooting guide

This airfield lighting troubleshooting guide takes you from symptom to cause: observe, identify the circuit,
isolate, measure, verify, correct and retest. The divisions of the Atlas give the detailed diagnostic records
for each type of fault.

### Airfield lighting fault diagnosis

Airfield lighting fault diagnosis separates the possible causes by looking at what is out, where, and at which
brightness step. Common-cause checks, such as the CCR, a feeder or a cable section, come before replacing
individual lights.

### Airfield ground lighting troubleshooting

Airfield ground lighting troubleshooting covers the whole chain: the CCR, series circuit, isolating
transformers, connectors, fixtures and control. Work from the symptom and prove the cause before changing
parts.

### Airfield lighting troubleshooting

Airfield lighting troubleshooting is a structured way to find why lights are out, dim, flickering or alarmed.
Safe isolation, measurement and records matter as much as technical knowledge.

### Airport lighting troubleshooting

Airport lighting troubleshooting brings together electrical, optical and control checks to restore the
lighting system. After repair, retest and record the result so the fix is confirmed.

## Frequently Asked Questions

Quick answers about the AGL Troubleshooting Atlas and its 30 divisions.

The AGL Troubleshooting Atlas is a 30-division diagnostic reference for airfield ground lighting. All 30
divisions are published, with 700 topics in total across equipment, circuit, installation, photometry,
control, operational, emergency and root-cause divisions. Each topic follows an 11-field diagnostic record.

The 30 divisions are grouped into nine categories: Equipment (11); Circuits & Electrical (5); Installation &
Commissioning (1); Photometry (1); Control & Monitoring (1); Operations & CAT (2); Diagnostics & RCA (4);
Emergency & Case Studies (2); Preventive & Reference (3). The page's filter tabs let you browse by category,
and the search box filters divisions by keyword or fault topic.

The Equipment category has 11 divisions: Division 01 CCR Troubleshooting; Division 03 Isolating Transformer
Troubleshooting; Division 04 Runway Edge Light Troubleshooting; Division 05 Runway Centreline Light
Troubleshooting; Division 06 Touchdown Zone Light Troubleshooting; Division 07 Taxiway Light Troubleshooting;
Division 08 Taxiway Centreline / Guidance Lighting; Division 09 Stop Bar / Guard Light Troubleshooting;
Division 10 Approach Lighting System Troubleshooting; Division 11 PAPI / VASI Troubleshooting; Division 12
Airfield Signage Troubleshooting.

The Circuits & Electrical category has 5 divisions: Division 02 AGL Series Circuit Troubleshooting; Division
13 AGL Cable Troubleshooting; Division 14 L-823 / Connector Troubleshooting; Division 15 Series Circuit
Electrical Faults; Division 16 Earthing / Lightning / Surge Troubleshooting.

Installation & Commissioning: Division 17 Installation & Commissioning Faults. Photometry: Division 18 AGL
Photometry Troubleshooting. Control & Monitoring: Division 19 ALCMS / Control & Monitoring. Operations & CAT:
Division 20 CAT I / CAT II / CAT III Troubleshooting; Division 21 Operational & Maintenance Problems.

Diagnostics & RCA: Division 22 Difficult / Intermittent Faults; Division 23 Root Cause Analysis / Failure
Investigation; Division 26 Advanced Diagnostic Topics; Division 29 Diagnostic Decision Trees. Preventive &
Reference: Division 27 Preventive Troubleshooting; Division 28 Troubleshooting Checklist Library; Division 30
Advanced RCA / Engineering Investigation.

Division 24 (Emergency Quick-diagnosis) gives fast diagnosis guides for total or partial lighting failure,
major faults and airport-wide communication loss. Division 29 (Diagnostic Decision Trees) gives structured
decision trees for CCR, circuit, transformer, connector, fixture and communication faults. For a specific
equipment fault, go straight to its equipment or circuit division.

Every topic follows the same diagnostic record: the symptom, equipment/system, possible causes ranked by
likelihood, required tools, safety precautions, diagnostic procedure, test points, root cause verification,
corrective action, preventive action and related references such as SOPs, standards, diagrams and case
studies.

Type a keyword such as 'earth fault', 'PAPI' or 'connector' into the search box to filter divisions and their
fault topics, or use the category tabs. Each division page also has its own search box for its topics.

An AGL maintenance checklist is a written list of the inspection, cleaning, testing and repair steps for a
type of lighting, signed off for each visit. It covers items such as lamp and lens condition, connector and
base can checks, CCR readings, insulation resistance and brightness steps, so that work is consistent and
recorded. The Troubleshooting Checklist Library (Division 28) holds ready-made checklists.

An airport lighting fault is found by working from the symptom to the faulty section. Start with the alarm or
the inspection report, check the CCR output current and brightness step, test the circuit for earth leakage
and continuity, then split the circuit to isolate the section. The final check is a field test of the
individual light, transformer or connector. Division 24 (Emergency Quick-diagnosis) and Division 29
(Diagnostic Decision Trees) set this out step by step.

Common causes of runway light failure are lamp burnout, moisture or flooding in the fixture, damaged
connectors, failed isolating transformers, cable insulation breakdown, surge or lightning damage, and impact
from vehicles or aircraft. If a whole circuit is out, check the CCR and main cable first. See Divisions 04,
05, 06 and 09 for the individual light types.

Taxiway light failure is usually caused by water in the fixture, lamp burnout, damaged base cans or
connectors, failed isolating transformers, and cable damage from excavation or heavy loads. Taxiway lights
also see more wheel loading and jet blast than most runway lights. See Divisions 07 and 08 for taxiway edge
and centreline lighting faults.

Signs of an AGL earth fault include a CCR earth fault alarm, a trip, or a low insulation resistance reading on
the circuit. With the circuit isolated and made safe, test insulation resistance and divide the circuit into
sections to find the faulty cable, connector or transformer. Follow the test method and limits in your
standard and manufacturer data.

## Airfield Lighting Diagnostics & Remote Diagnostics

### Airfield lighting system diagnostics

Airfield lighting system diagnostics is the process of finding why part of the lighting system is not working
as it should. It combines the symptom, the circuit and equipment concerned, field measurements and the control
system status. The engine above guides this step by step, from symptom to likely cause and the tests that
confirm it.

### Airfield lighting remote diagnostics

Airfield lighting remote diagnostics uses the control and monitoring system, CCR status, alarms and event logs
to narrow down a fault without going to the field first. It saves time and helps decide who to send and what
to carry, but the fault should still be confirmed and the repair checked on site.

### AGL Failure Database | 25-Division Root Cause Repository

Canonical URL: https://rahulsharmaagl.in/failure-database.html

**Page summary:** A database of AGL failures across 25 engineering divisions, each record covering what happened, root cause, evidence, corrective action and prevention.

# AGL Failure Database

A structured historical and analytical repository of AGL failures, organised into 25 engineering divisions —
covering equipment, circuits, installation, environment, control systems, operations, reliability and root-
cause investigation. Every failure record answers one question: this failure happened — what happened, why did
it happen, what evidence proves it, what was done, and how do we prevent it happening again?

Distinct from the Troubleshooting Atlas — the Atlas answers “I have a fault now, how do I diagnose and fix
it?”, while the Failure Database is the historical, evidence-backed record of failures already investigated.

## Browse by Division

Search by keyword or filter by category. Divisions range from equipment- and circuit-specific failure
catalogues through to root-cause methodology, severity classification, reliability trending, and the master
failure-record architecture.

#### Lighting Fixture Failures

Runway and taxiway fixture failures, plus core component failures — LED modules, drivers, lenses, seals, and
housings.

#### Electrical Failures

Cable insulation breakdown, open/short circuits, earth faults, connector failures, and other core electrical
failure modes.

#### CCR Failures

CCR output instability, thyristor and controller failures, protection trips, communication faults, and
cooling-system failures.

#### Isolation Transformer Failures

Isolation transformer insulation breakdown, winding and core damage, water ingress, overheating, and
terminal/lead failures.

#### Cable & Connector Failures

Cable degradation, joint and termination failures, plus connector corrosion, contact resistance, and
seal/locking failures.

#### Mechanical & Structural Failures

Base-can corrosion, frangible-coupling failure, loose mounting, foundation settlement, and structural/hardware
damage.

#### Control System Failures

PLC and SCADA faults, network and communication failures, HMI and control-panel failures, and control-logic
errors.

#### Human & Installation Failures

Installation, testing/commissioning, maintenance, and documentation errors that originate from human and
procedural factors.

#### Environmental Failures

Lightning, flooding, sand, snow/ice, UV, salt corrosion, and other weather- and environment-driven failure
modes.

#### Operational Incidents

Runway/taxiway outages, multiple-circuit failures, wildlife and vehicle impact, and other operational
disruption events.

#### PAPI / APAPI Failures

PAPI/APAPI unit, lamp/LED, alignment, elevation/azimuth, and optical-window failures affecting glide-path
indication.

#### Airfield Sign Failures

Airfield sign LED module, driver, illumination, mounting, and structural failures across taxiway and runway
signage.

#### Approach Lighting Failures

Approach lighting fixture, crossbar, pole, and foundation failures, plus optical, circuit, and weather-related
damage.

#### Stop Bar & Runway Guard Light Failures

Stop bar and runway guard light illumination, flashing, control, alignment, and structural failure modes.

#### Earthing & Bonding Failures

Earth-continuity and bonding failures across fixtures, transformers, signs, CCRs, and lightning/surge
protection systems.

#### Base Can & Civil Interface Failures

Base-can and civil-interface failures — corrosion, flooding, drainage, foundation, and cable-entry/sealing
problems.

#### Testing & Commissioning Failures

Insulation-resistance, continuity, earth-resistance, functional, photometric, and acceptance test failures at
commissioning.

#### Maintenance-Induced Failures

Failures introduced during maintenance — incorrect procedures, torque, sealing, calibration, spares, and
documentation gaps.

#### Product & Component Reliability Failures

Premature component failure, manufacturing/design defects, supplier-quality issues, and product-
life/obsolescence trends.

#### Emerging Technology Failures

LED-system degradation, smart-sensor and IoT faults, cybersecurity issues, and software/firmware and digital-
twin errors.

#### Root Cause Analysis Database

Structured RCA categories — electrical, mechanical, human, procedural — plus 5-Why, fishbone, and fault-tree
methods.

#### Failure Severity & Criticality

Severity and criticality classification, from safety-critical to non-critical, and operational, financial, and
downtime impact.

#### Reliability & Failure Trend Analysis

Failure-rate, MTBF/MTTR, and availability metrics, plus monthly/seasonal trend analysis and failure-hotspot

#### Corrective Action, Preventive Action & Lessons Learned

Immediate, temporary, and permanent corrective actions; preventive-action programs; and structured lessons-

- Revision History

### Failure Database vs. Troubleshooting Atlas

The Troubleshooting Atlas answers “I have a fault now — how do I diagnose and fix it?” The Failure Database
answers “this failure happened — what happened, why, what evidence proves it, what was done, and how do we
stop it recurring?” Kept strictly separate, then linked end-to-end, the two form a genuine AGL Failure
Intelligence Engine rather than a simple fault list.

# AGL Inspection Handbook

A division-wise reference for what to inspect on an installed AGL system — not how to install or repair it.
Every division answers one question: for this asset, what must be verified, against what standard, and how is
the result classified? Built around a five-level inspection hierarchy, from daily walk-arounds to full
airport-wide condition audits.

All 25 divisions are now live, covering 1,173 published inspection topics across the full AGL asset base.

How this differs from the SOP Library: the SOP Library documents procedure — how to install, test, or repair.
This handbook documents inspection — what to verify on equipment that is already installed, how to compare it
against tolerance, and how to classify and record what's found. Philosophy: observe → verify → compare →
classify → record → action.

## Five-Level Inspection Hierarchy

Every inspection topic in the handbook sits at one of five levels, from routine daily checks through to a
complete airport-wide AGL audit. The level sets the frequency, the trigger, and how deep the inspection goes.

#### Routine Inspection

Operational-condition checks confirming the system is serviceable right now.

#### Detailed Equipment Inspection

Component-level checks going beyond visual status into condition, calibration, and record review.

#### Special Inspection

Follows failure, lightning, flooding, major maintenance, construction, an accident/incident, or severe
weather.

#### Acceptance Inspection

For new installation, replacement, modification, rehabilitation, or commissioning of AGL assets.

#### AGL System Audit

Complete airport-level assessment spanning runway, taxiway, approach, PAPI, signs, CCR, transformers, cables,
connectors, earthing, ALCMS, and documentation.

## How an Inspection Topic Works

Each topic in the handbook follows the same six-step logic, whatever the asset or level.

### Runway Edge Light — Inspection Point Example

A handbook topic isn't "how to install a runway edge light" — it's the full set of points checked on a light
that's already in service, each with a defined pass condition.

Inspection Point | What to Verify

Fixture position | Correct location

Alignment | Correct orientation

Height | Within required installation tolerance

Lens | Clean and undamaged

Housing | No damage/corrosion

Mounting | Secure

Frangible coupling | Correct condition

Cable | No visible damage

Connector | Secure and sealed

Illumination | Correct operation

Identification | Correct asset/circuit marking

Surrounding area | No FOD/obstruction

Water | No unacceptable accumulation

## Defect Classification

Every finding is classified consistently across all 25 divisions, so severity means the same thing whether
it's a runway light or a CCR cabinet.

#### Critical

Directly affects flight safety or immediate serviceability. Requires immediate action.

#### Major

Significant deterioration or non-conformance that must be corrected within a defined short window.

#### Minor

Does not affect operational serviceability but should be tracked and scheduled for correction.

#### Observation

Noted for awareness and trend tracking — no immediate corrective action required.
