### AGL Maintenance Handbook: Preventive, Corrective, Predictive

Canonical URL: https://rahulsharmaagl.in/maintenance-handbook.html

**Page summary:** AGL maintenance handbook: runway edge lights, centreline lights and threshold lights preventive maintenance, plus corrective and predictive strategies.

# AGL Maintenance Handbook

A strategy-wise reference for keeping an installed AGL system serviceable — not how to install it, and not
what to verify on it, but what maintenance to actually perform, when, and why. Organized across 25 divisions
spanning maintenance strategy, asset type, and the planning and records that hold the programme together.

All 25 divisions (835 topics) are published.

How this differs from the other references: the SOP Library documents procedure — how to install, test, or
repair. The Inspection Handbook documents verification — what to check on equipment already in service. This
handbook documents the maintenance decision itself — which strategy applies (preventive, corrective,
predictive, condition-based, or emergency), and the specific task that strategy calls for on every AGL asset.

## Five Maintenance Strategies

Every maintenance topic in the handbook is driven by one of five strategies. The strategy sets the trigger,
the timing, and how the work gets authorised and closed.

#### Preventive

Scheduled, routine work — cleaning, tightening, alignment, and functional checks — performed regardless of
condition to prevent failure.

#### Corrective

Repair or replacement once an inspection, failure, or abnormal condition has confirmed a specific defect.

#### Predictive

Condition and performance data tracked over time — insulation resistance, CCR output, LED degradation — to
forecast failure before it happens.

#### Condition-Based

Work scoped to the asset's actual measured condition rather than a fixed interval — physical, environmental,
and performance state decide what's justified.

#### Emergency

Rapid-response work for critical AGL failures affecting runway or approach availability — distinct in urgency,
authorisation, and reporting from routine corrective work.

## Runway Light Preventive Maintenance

Preventive work on the main runway lights follows the interval-driven approach described above. These are the
three runway circuits most often scheduled first.

### Runway Edge Lights Preventive Maintenance

Scheduled cleaning of lenses, checking of fixture mounting and alignment, connector and seal checks and
functional checks along the runway edge circuits, before faults develop.

### Runway Centreline Lights Preventive Maintenance

Routine inspection of inset fixtures, lens condition, sealing and fixing, and functional checks of the
centreline circuits, including after heavy-wheel traffic and pavement works.

### Threshold Lights Preventive Maintenance

Scheduled checks of threshold and wing bar lights: cleaning, alignment, colour and output checks, connector
condition and circuit function.

## Maintenance Record Flow

Every maintenance topic in the handbook follows the same record, from what triggered the work through to what
closes it out.

## Browse by Division

Divisions 01–05 cover the five maintenance strategies. Divisions 06–20 cover equipment-, asset- and interface-
specific maintenance. Divisions 21–25 cover documentation, spares, testing, planning, and audit. All procedure
pages are now published; each card below shows the number of topics covered.

#### Preventive Maintenance

The routine, calendar-driven backbone of the handbook — cleaning, tightening, alignment, and functional checks
on every AGL asset.

#### Corrective Maintenance

Repair or replacement work triggered once an inspection, failure, or abnormal condition has confirmed a
defect.

#### Predictive Maintenance

Condition- and trend-based forecasting — insulation resistance, CCR output, and LED performance tracked over
time to flag failure before it happens.

#### Condition-Based Maintenance

Maintenance scoped to actual asset condition rather than the calendar — physical, environmental, and
performance state decide what work is justified.

#### Emergency Maintenance

Rapid-response work for critical AGL failures — distinct from routine corrective maintenance in urgency,
authorisation, and reporting.

#### Lighting Fixture Maintenance

Mechanical, optical, and electrical upkeep of every physical light fixture, independent of where it sits on
the airfield.

#### CCR Maintenance

External, internal, and control-system maintenance for Constant Current Regulators, including performance
verification.

#### Isolation Transformer Maintenance

Routine and corrective maintenance for isolation transformers, plus pit and installation condition checks.

#### Cable Maintenance

Route, condition, joint, and termination maintenance across the primary AGL cable network, through to testing
and restoration.

#### Connector Maintenance

Inspection, cleaning, and corrective work on L-823 connectors — electrical condition, installation, and
protection.

#### Inspection-Driven Maintenance

The direct bridge from the Inspection Handbook into maintenance work — findings, closure, and condition
escalation.

#### Asset-Specific Maintenance

Equipment-level service guidance organised by asset type, from runway and taxiway assets through to control
systems.

#### PAPI / APAPI Maintenance

Preventive, corrective, and performance maintenance covering PAPI/APAPI optical and mechanical condition.

#### Airfield Sign Maintenance

Preventive, corrective, and special maintenance for airfield signage — LED modules, drivers, and structural
condition.

#### Cable & Connector Maintenance

The complete primary cable → joint → transformer → secondary lead → connector → fixture maintenance chain.

#### Earthing & Bonding Maintenance

Earthing system, equipment bonding, and lightning/surge protection maintenance, with associated testing.

#### ALCMS & Control System Maintenance

Preventive, corrective, and functional maintenance for control, monitoring, and communication equipment.

#### Approach Lighting Maintenance

Preventive, corrective, and special maintenance across the approach lighting system.

#### Stop Bar & Runway Guard Light Maintenance

Maintenance specific to stop bar and runway guard light circuits and fixtures.

#### Base Can & Civil Interface Maintenance

Base can, civil interface, and post-maintenance restoration work at the fixture-to-ground interface.

#### Documentation & Maintenance Records

Maintenance, testing, and asset records, plus the document control that keeps them traceable.

#### Spare Parts & Asset Lifecycle Maintenance

Spare parts management and equipment lifecycle tracking, with a dedicated focus on critical AGL spares.

#### Post-Maintenance Testing & Restoration

The bridge between maintenance and return to service — electrical testing, functional testing, photometry, and
restoration.

#### Maintenance Planning & Scheduling

When, why, and how maintenance work is planned — asset-based prioritisation, work planning, and schedule
control.

#### Maintenance Audit & Continuous Improvement

The management and reliability division — audit, failure analysis, reliability metrics, and continuous
improvement.

### AGL Testing & Commissioning Manual | 514 Topics

Canonical URL: https://rahulsharmaagl.in/testing-commissioning-manual.html

**Page summary:** A 25-division, 514-topic reference for AGL testing and commissioning: electrical, functional, photometric and integration checks from readiness to handover.

# AGL Testing & Commissioning Manual

A performance-verification reference for AGL systems — not whether the installation is physically correct, not
how to keep it running, and not what's causing a fault, but whether the installed system electrically,
functionally, photometrically, and integrally performs as required. Organized across 25 divisions spanning
pre-commissioning readiness, component and system-level testing, factory and site acceptance, integration,
performance, troubleshooting, documentation, handover, and advanced commissioning.

Master structure is complete across all 25 divisions (514 topics) , and all 25 divisions are now published in
full.

How this differs from the other references: the Inspection Handbook asks whether the installation is
physically correct and in acceptable condition. The Maintenance Handbook documents how to keep an accepted
system operational. The Troubleshooting Atlas diagnoses what's causing a failure. This manual asks a different
question entirely — does the installed system electrically, functionally, photometrically, and integrally
perform as required, from first energization through final handover.

## Three References, Three Questions

The same AGL asset can appear in four different references for four different reasons. This manual sits at the
commissioning stage — after installation, before the system is accepted into service.

#### Is it physically correct?

Verification of equipment already in service — condition, alignment, and physical state against standard.

#### Does it perform as required?

Electrical, functional, photometric, and system-integration proof that the installed system meets
specification before acceptance.

#### How do we keep it running?

The maintenance strategy and specific task that applies to an accepted, in-service asset.

#### What's causing the failure?

Fault diagnosis and root-cause investigation once something has already gone wrong.

## Commissioning Lifecycle

The 25 divisions follow a single lifecycle, from readiness review through to final handover — component and
system testing form the bulk of the manual, bracketed by acceptance testing on either side.

## Browse by Division

Divisions 01–16 cover pre-commissioning readiness and component/system-level testing by equipment type.
Divisions 17–20 cover acceptance testing, integration, and performance. Divisions 21–25 cover troubleshooting,
documentation, handover, advanced commissioning, and test-equipment quality. Topic scope is set for every
division; full procedure content is being published division by division.

#### Pre-Commissioning Verification

Focus: Verify that the installation is ready for testing — before energization, before testing, before
commissioning begins.

#### Electrical Testing

The core electrical-test division — insulation, continuity, earth, voltage, current, and cable testing across
every AGL circuit.

#### CCR Testing & Commissioning

Full CCR test and commissioning scope — input supply, output regulation, step transitions, protections,
alarms, and remote/local control.

#### Isolation Transformer Testing & Commissioning

Visual, electrical, and acceptance testing for isolation transformers, from nameplate verification through
loading and output.

#### Airfield Lighting Fixture Testing

Installation, alignment, optical, and operational testing for runway, taxiway, and approach lighting fixtures.

#### Runway Lighting System Commissioning

System-level commissioning for edge, threshold, end, centreline, touchdown-zone, and runway guard-light
circuits.

#### Taxiway Lighting System Commissioning

Commissioning for taxiway edge, centreline, clearance-bar, exit, and rapid-exit taxiway lighting circuits.

#### Approach Lighting System Commissioning

Structural, electrical, and photometric commissioning of the complete approach lighting system.

#### PAPI / APAPI Testing & Commissioning

Installation, alignment, calibration, and acceptance testing for PAPI and APAPI units.

#### Airfield Sign Testing & Commissioning

Electrical, illumination, and message verification for airfield guidance signs.

#### Stop Bar & Runway Guard Light Testing

Electrical, flashing-operation, and control testing across stop bars and runway guard lights.

#### Cable & Connector Testing

Continuity, insulation, and termination testing across cables and connectors network-wide.

#### Earthing & Bonding Testing

Earth-pit, electrode, conductor, and bonding verification across every earthed AGL asset.

#### Monitoring, Control & ALCMS Testing

SCADA, PLC, HMI, and ALCMS integration testing — remote monitoring, alarms, control interfaces, and
interlocking.

#### Functional Testing

How the complete system behaves in operation — switching logic, interlocks, sequencing, and failure response.

#### Photometric Testing

Intensity, beam alignment, colour, uniformity, and distribution testing across every lit asset type.

#### Factory Acceptance Testing (FAT)

Pre-delivery witness testing at the manufacturer — electrical, functional, performance, and protection
testing.

#### Site Acceptance Testing (SAT)

On-site witness testing following installation — integration, control, alarm, and photometric testing.

#### System Integration Testing

CCR-to-ALCMS, PLC, SCADA, and network integration — command/feedback, redundancy, and integrated emergency
operation.

#### Performance Acceptance Testing

Whole-system performance verification against project specification, asset by asset.

#### Troubleshooting During Commissioning

Fault identification, isolation, root-cause analysis, corrective action, and retesting during commissioning.

#### Commissioning Documentation

Every report, certificate, and record the commissioning process produces, through to the final dossier.

#### Handover & Final Acceptance

Final review, outstanding punch/snag closure, training verification, and handover certification.

#### Advanced Commissioning

LED performance, smart AGL systems, remote diagnostics, and cybersecurity checks for networked equipment.

#### Test Equipment, Calibration & Engineering Quality

Test equipment guides, calibration control, and the quality checks that keep every test result defensible.

## Frequently Asked Questions

Quick answers about the AGL Testing & Commissioning Manual and how its 25 divisions fit together.

The AGL Testing & Commissioning Manual is a performance-verification reference for AGL systems — not whether
the installation is physically correct, not how to keep it running, and not what's causing a fault, but
whether the installed system electrically, functionally, photometrically, and integrally performs as required.
Organized across 25 divisions spanning pre-commissioning readiness, component and system-level testing,
factory and site acceptance, integration, performance, troubleshooting, documentation, handover, and advanced
commissioning.

The Inspection Handbook asks whether the installation is physically correct and in acceptable condition. The
Maintenance Handbook documents how to keep an accepted system operational. The Troubleshooting Atlas diagnoses
what is causing a failure. The Testing & Commissioning Manual asks a different question: does the installed
system electrically, functionally, photometrically and integrally perform as required, from first energization
through final handover?

Divisions 01–16 cover pre-commissioning readiness and component and system-level testing by equipment type.
Divisions 17–20 cover acceptance testing, integration and performance. Divisions 21–25 cover troubleshooting,
documentation, handover, advanced commissioning and test-equipment quality. The full list is: Division 01 —
Pre-Commissioning Verification; Division 02 — Electrical Testing; Division 03 — CCR Testing & Commissioning;
Division 04 — Isolation Transformer Testing & Commissioning; Division 05 — Airfield Lighting Fixture Testing;
Division 06 — Runway Lighting System Commissioning; Division 07 — Taxiway Lighting System Commissioning;
Division 08 — Approach Lighting System Commissioning; Division 09 — PAPI / APAPI Testing & Commissioning;
Division 10 — Airfield Sign Testing & Commissioning; Division 11 — Stop Bar & Runway Guard Light Testing;
Division 12 — Cable & Connector Testing; Division 13 — Earthing & Bonding Testing; Division 14 — Monitoring,
Control & ALCMS Testing; Division 15 — Functional Testing; Division 16 — Photometric Testing; Division 17 —
Factory Acceptance Testing (FAT); Division 18 — Site Acceptance Testing (SAT); Division 19 — System
Integration Testing; Division 20 — Performance Acceptance Testing; Division 21 — Troubleshooting During
Commissioning; Division 22 — Commissioning Documentation; Division 23 — Handover & Final Acceptance; Division
24 — Advanced Commissioning; Division 25 — Test Equipment, Calibration & Engineering Quality.

The 25 divisions follow a single lifecycle: 01 Pre-Commissioning, then 02–16 Component & System Testing, 17
FAT, 18 SAT, 19 System Integration, 20 Performance Acceptance, 21 Troubleshooting & Retesting, 22
Documentation, 23 Handover & Final Acceptance, 24 Advanced Commissioning and 25 Test Equipment & Quality.
Component and system testing form the bulk of the manual, bracketed by acceptance testing on either side.

With Division 01 — Pre-Commissioning Verification, whose focus is to verify that the installation is ready for
testing — before energization, before testing, before commissioning begins. Division 02 onward then covers the
equipment-specific testing, starting with electrical testing.

Divisions 02–16 do: Division 02 — Electrical Testing (the core electrical-test division — insulation,
continuity, earth, voltage, current, and cable testing across every AGL circuit); Division 03 — CCR Testing &
Commissioning (full CCR test and commissioning scope — input supply, output regulation, step transitions,
protections, alarms, and remote/local control); Division 04 — Isolation Transformer Testing & Commissioning
(visual, electrical, and acceptance testing for isolation transformers, from nameplate verification through
loading and output); Division 05 — Airfield Lighting Fixture Testing (installation, alignment, optical, and
operational testing for runway, taxiway, and approach lighting fixtures); Division 06 — Runway Lighting System
Commissioning (system-level commissioning for edge, threshold, end, centreline, touchdown-zone, and runway
guard-light circuits); Division 07 — Taxiway Lighting System Commissioning (commissioning for taxiway edge,
centreline, clearance-bar, exit, and rapid-exit taxiway lighting circuits); Division 08 — Approach Lighting
System Commissioning (structural, electrical, and photometric commissioning of the complete approach lighting
system); Division 09 — PAPI / APAPI Testing & Commissioning (installation, alignment, calibration, and
acceptance testing for PAPI and APAPI units); Division 10 — Airfield Sign Testing & Commissioning (electrical,
illumination, and message verification for airfield guidance signs); Division 11 — Stop Bar & Runway Guard
Light Testing (electrical, flashing-operation, and control testing across stop bars and runway guard lights);
Division 12 — Cable & Connector Testing (continuity, insulation, and termination testing across cables and
connectors network-wide); Division 13 — Earthing & Bonding Testing (earth-pit, electrode, conductor, and
bonding verification across every earthed AGL asset); Division 14 — Monitoring, Control & ALCMS Testing
(SCADA, PLC, HMI, and ALCMS integration testing — remote monitoring, alarms, control interfaces, and
interlocking); Division 15 — Functional Testing (how the complete system behaves in operation — switching
logic, interlocks, sequencing, and failure response); Division 16 — Photometric Testing (intensity, beam
alignment, colour, uniformity, and distribution testing across every lit asset type).

Division 17 (FAT) is pre-delivery witness testing at the manufacturer — electrical, functional, performance,
and protection testing. Division 18 (SAT) is on-site witness testing following installation — integration,
control, alarm, and photometric testing. FAT comes before SAT in the lifecycle, and both sit between component
and system testing and the integration and performance divisions.

Division 19 — System Integration Testing: CCR-to-ALCMS, PLC, SCADA, and network integration —
command/feedback, redundancy, and integrated emergency operation. Division 20 — Performance Acceptance
Testing: whole-system performance verification against project specification, asset by asset. Division 21 —
Troubleshooting During Commissioning: fault identification, isolation, root-cause analysis, corrective action,
and retesting during commissioning.

Division 22 — Commissioning Documentation: every report, certificate, and record the commissioning process
produces, through to the final dossier. Division 23 — Handover & Final Acceptance: final review, outstanding
punch/snag closure, training verification, and handover certification. Division 24 — Advanced Commissioning:
LED performance, smart AGL systems, remote diagnostics, and cybersecurity checks for networked equipment.

Division 25 — Test Equipment, Calibration & Engineering Quality: test equipment guides, calibration control,
and the quality checks that keep every test result defensible.

## 25 Divisions of Testing & Commissioning. One Skill That Ties Them Together.

This manual tells you what to verify, test, and record at every stage. It doesn't teach you why each check
exists or how the underlying engineering actually works.

### AGL Asset Lifecycle Guide | 25 Divisions, 495 Topics

Canonical URL: https://rahulsharmaagl.in/asset-lifecycle-guide.html

**Page summary:** The strategic asset-management layer for AGL, from planning to disposal: 25 divisions, 495 topics on criticality, lifecycle cost, reliability and replacement.

# AGL Asset Lifecycle Guide

The strategic layer of the AGL Knowledge Hub — not whether an asset is installed correctly, not how to keep it
running, not why it failed, but what should be done with it throughout its entire life. Organized across 25
divisions spanning planning, criticality, procurement, installation, commissioning, operations, maintenance
strategy, health monitoring, reliability, lifecycle cost, spares, refurbishment, replacement, decommissioning,
and digital asset management.

All 25 divisions (495 topics) are structured and published.

How this differs from the other references: the Inspection Handbook asks whether the installation is
physically correct. The Testing & Commissioning Manual asks whether it performs as required. The Maintenance
Handbook documents how to keep an accepted, in-service asset running. The Failure Database explains why
something failed and how to prevent recurrence. This guide sits above all four — it's the strategic layer that
decides what to do with an asset from the day it's planned to the day it's recycled, and it's what ties the
other four references together.

## Five References, Five Questions

The same AGL asset can appear in five different references for five different reasons. This guide is the only
one that spans the full life — the other four each own one stage or one lens.

#### Is it physically correct?

Condition, alignment, and physical state of equipment already in service, against standard.

#### Does it perform as required?

Electrical, functional, photometric, and integration proof before acceptance into service.

#### How do we keep it running?

The maintenance strategy and specific task that applies to an accepted, in-service asset.

#### Why did it fail?

Root-cause investigation and recurrence-prevention once something has already gone wrong.

#### What should we do with it?

The strategic decision layer — plan, procure, operate, maintain, refurbish, replace, or dispose — across the
asset's entire life.

## The Asset Lifecycle Flow

The central logic of the guide: every asset moves through these twelve stages, and every division below maps
onto one or more of them.

## How It Connects

The guide doesn't replace the other four references — it's the spine they attach to.

AGL Design Manual | Division 04 (Design for Lifecycle Performance) feeds design-stage decisions — maintainability, reliability, standardization, and lifecycle cost — back into design practice.

AGL Testing & Commissioning Manual | Division 07 (Commissioning & Baseline Asset Performance) establishes the baseline every later health, reliability, and condition assessment is measured against.

AGL Maintenance Handbook | Division 09 (Maintenance Strategy & Optimization) stays strategic — strategy selection and optimization — while the Handbook owns the day-to-day procedure.

AGL Inspection Handbook | Division 15 (Asset Inspection & Condition Assessment) feeds condition grades and defect data directly into the asset health index.

AGL Failure Database | Division 11 (Reliability Engineering & Failure Management) is the lifecycle-level home for MTBF, MTTR, and failure-trend data.

AGL Asset Lifecycle Guide | What should we do with this asset throughout its entire life? — the question every other division answers a piece of.

## Browse by Division

Divisions 01–07 cover the front half of the lifecycle — planning through baseline performance. Divisions 08–15
cover operations, maintenance strategy, health, reliability, cost, spares, and warranty. Divisions 16–20 cover
refurbishment, upgrade, obsolescence, replacement, and disposal. Divisions 21–25 cover digital asset
management, KPIs, audit, case studies, and the master asset-record database.

#### Asset Planning & Strategy

Where the lifecycle starts — identification, classification, coding, criticality, and long-term asset
strategy.

#### Asset Register & Data Management

The structure of the master register — identification fields, dates, condition, history links, and data
governance.

#### Asset Criticality & Risk Assessment

Criticality methodology and risk ranking for runway, taxiway, PAPI, CCR, transformer, cable, sign and ALCMS
assets.

#### Design for Lifecycle Performance

Connects the Asset Lifecycle Guide with the AGL Design Manual — maintainability, reliability, and lifecycle-
cost in design.

#### Procurement & Vendor Management

Design-life expectations, product selection, vendor evaluation, spare-parts strategy, and warranty management.

#### Installation & Asset Handover

Installation records, commissioning documentation, baseline performance, and asset handover to operations.

#### Commissioning & Baseline Asset Performance

Establishes the baseline every later assessment is measured against — connects directly with Testing &
Commissioning.

#### Operations & Asset Performance

Utilization, availability, energy consumption, and performance trending during in-service operation.

#### Maintenance Strategy & Optimization

Where lifecycle strategy meets the Maintenance Handbook — strategy selection and optimization, not procedure.

#### Asset Health Monitoring

Condition scoring, health index, degradation monitoring, and Remaining Useful Life estimation.

#### Reliability Engineering & Failure Management

The lifecycle-level connection to the Failure Database — MTBF, MTTR, failure trends, and reliability-centred
maintenance.

#### Asset Lifecycle Cost Management

A major division — lifecycle decisions should never be based on purchase price alone. Total cost of ownership,
forecasting, optimization.

#### Spare Parts & Inventory Lifecycle

Stock levels, critical-spare identification, obsolete-spare management, and inventory optimization.

#### Warranty & Supplier Lifecycle Management

Warranty tracking, claims, supplier performance and reliability trends, and post-warranty support.

#### Asset Inspection & Condition Assessment

Connects directly with the AGL Inspection Handbook — condition grading and defect classification feed the
health index.

#### Refurbishment & Life Extension

Life-extension programmes, retrofit planning, modernization, and refurbish-versus-replace decisions.

#### Technology Upgrade & Modernization

LED conversion, smart AGL, digital control, remote monitoring, and upgrade business cases.

#### Obsolescence Management

Identifying and managing discontinued products, legacy systems, and last-time-buy decisions.

#### Replacement Planning & Decision Making

One of the most important divisions — replacement triggers, decision matrices, and long-term replacement
programmes.

#### Decommissioning, Disposal & Recycling

Isolation, removal, e-waste management, recycling records, and final asset-register closure.

#### Digital Asset Management

CMMS/EAM, digital twins, IoT monitoring, predictive analytics, and AI-based asset optimization.

#### Asset Performance & KPI Management

The full KPI set — availability, reliability, MTBF, MTTR, lifecycle cost, and dashboard reporting.

#### Asset Audit & Governance

Asset audit checklists across the register, criticality, maintenance, inspection, testing, and disposal
records.

#### Lifecycle Case Studies & Decision Models

Real lifecycle case studies across every flagship asset type, plus repair-vs-replace and capital-investment
decision models.

#### Asset Lifecycle Master Database & Intelligence

The master data layer — the 29-field standard asset record every AGL asset should carry, from Asset ID to
disposal status.

#### Recommended flagship asset series

The guide is built to be populated asset-by-asset, starting with runway edge lights, taxiway lights, approach
lighting, airfield signs, CCRs, isolation transformers, primary/secondary cables, base cans, cable ducts,
handholes and foundations — followed by asset health monitoring, reliability engineering, replacement
planning, lifecycle-cost optimization, and digital asset management.

## Frequently Asked Questions

Quick answers about the AGL Asset Lifecycle Guide and how its 25 divisions fit together.

It is the strategic asset-management layer of the AGL Knowledge Hub, covering what should be done with every
airfield ground lighting asset from planning through disposal. It is organized into 25 divisions and 495
topics, all published.

The Inspection Handbook asks whether the installation is physically correct, the Testing & Commissioning
Manual asks whether it performs as required, the Maintenance Handbook covers how to keep an in-service asset
running, and the Failure Database explains why something failed. The Asset Lifecycle Guide sits above all four
and asks what should be done with the asset throughout its entire life.

Twelve stages: plan, design, procure, install, commission, operate, maintain, monitor health, repair,
refurbish or upgrade, replace, decommission, and dispose or recycle. Every division maps onto one or more of
them.

Divisions 01 to 07 cover the front half of the lifecycle, from planning through baseline performance.
Divisions 08 to 15 cover operations, maintenance strategy, health, reliability, cost, spares, warranty and
inspection. Divisions 16 to 20 cover refurbishment, upgrade, obsolescence, replacement and disposal. Divisions

Division 01, Asset Planning & Strategy, is the starting point of the lifecycle. From there Division 02 covers

## Airfield Ground Lighting Products & Systems

A structured portfolio of airfield lighting, visual aids, series-circuit equipment and technical equipment. We
help airports, consultants and contractors select, source, integrate, test and support the right products for
each application.

### From the approach path to the runway, taxiway and stand

Our product portfolio is organised by aviation application instead of isolated part numbers, and mapped
against ICAO Annex 14 and FAA AC 150/5340 designations wherever a recognised equivalent exists. This makes it
easier to identify the lighting system, electrical infrastructure and technical tools required for a complete
AGL installation.

### Runway Lighting Systems

Lighting systems that define runway edges, centreline, threshold, runway end and touchdown zones for different
operating and visibility conditions, up to CAT I / II / III precision approach runways.

### Taxiway & Apron Lighting

Visual guidance for aircraft movement from runway exits through taxiways, holding positions, rapid exits and
apron manoeuvring areas.

### Approach Lighting Systems

Approach and runway-entry visual guidance covering centreline, crossbar, side-row, threshold and sequenced
flashing applications for non-precision and precision approach categories.

### PAPI & Accessories

Precision approach path indicators together with the check, measurement and alignment accessories used to set
up and verify them.

### Airfield Guidance Signs & Markers

Illuminated signs and runway identification products for movement-area guidance and visual information.

### AGL Series Circuit Power & Connectivity

The electrical backbone of series-circuit airfield lighting, from CCR output through isolating transformers,
primary and secondary connector kits, cable and field termination.

### Wind Direction Indicators & Meteorological Aids

Visual wind indication and the sensor equipment that feeds airport meteorological and visibility reporting
systems.

### Obstruction & Identification Lighting

Lighting solutions used to improve the conspicuity of aviation obstacles, structures and airfield facilities.

### AGL Civil & Field Infrastructure

Installation hardware and field infrastructure required to position, protect, connect and maintain airfield
lighting equipment.

### AGL Spares, Retrofit & Replacement Equipment

Project-focused support for maintenance teams that need compatible replacement products, spares, upgrades and
retrofit options for existing airfield systems.

### Every product family should answer the engineering questions

Product pages should move beyond a photo and short description. Our technical format is designed around the

### Function, ICAO Annex 14 and FAA AC 150/5340 equivalence

A quick-reference map between lighting function and the two designation systems most commonly seen on
drawings, tenders and datasheets. Use it as an orientation aid — the applicable project specification always
governs the exact type, colour and intensity selected.

Function | ICAO Annex 14 designation | FAA equivalent (AC 150/5345 fixture types)

Runway edge light | Elevated / inset, white (yellow over the last 600 m or last third of the runway, whichever is less, on instrument runways) | L-850C (inset) / L-862 (elevated, high-intensity) or L-861 (elevated, medium-intensity)

Runway centreline | Inset, white / alternating red-white / red | L-850A (inset)

Runway threshold / end | Green (threshold) / red (end) | L-850D(L) (inset) / L-862E (elevated, high-intensity) or L-861E (elevated, medium-intensity)

Touchdown zone (TDZ) | White, paired barrettes | L-850B(L) (inset)

Taxiway centreline | Green (all) / alternating green-yellow near runway | L-852 series

Taxiway edge | Blue, omnidirectional | L-861T(L) (elevated) / L-852T(L) (inset)

Stop bar | Red, unidirectional, switchable | L-852S(L) (inset) / L-862S(L) (elevated)

Runway guard light | Alternating yellow, elevated / inset | L-804 (elevated) / L-852G(L) (inset)

Approach lighting system | SALS / MALS / precision approach configurations | ALSF-1 / ALSF-2 / MALSR / MALSF

Visual approach slope indicator | PAPI / APAPI | L-880 / L-881

Airfield guidance sign | Mandatory / information / direction signs | L-858

Obstacle / obstruction light | Low / medium / high intensity, Type A/B/C | L-810 (low, steady red) / L-864 and L-865 (medium) / L-856 and L-857 (high)

Series circuit isolating transformer | Series circuit transformer, per current rating | L-830 (60 Hz) / L-831 (50 Hz)

Primary connector / cable | Field connector kit, per circuit rating | L-823 / L-824

Designations are cited for general technical orientation only. ICAO and FAA numbering, colours and intensity
classes evolve between document revisions — always confirm the current designation against the latest ICAO
Annex 14 / Aerodrome Design Manual and FAA AC 150/5340 edition applicable to the project.

### AGL Applications: Airfield Ground Lighting by Airport Type

Canonical URL: https://rahulsharmaagl.in/agl-applications.html

**Page summary:** How Airfield Ground Lighting needs differ across commercial, international, military, regional and general aviation airports, heliports and retrofits.

# AGL APPLICATIONS

Airfield Ground Lighting is not a single, fixed specification. What a commercial hub needs, a regional strip,
a military airfield, a heliport or a disaster-relief runway needs are all different — in scale, redundancy,
category of operation and budget. This page walks through how AGL requirements change by airport type and
project type, and links to a dedicated guide for each.

## One System, Many Contexts

The fundamentals of AGL don't change — but the application does. A runway's ICAO reference code, its category
of approach (non-precision, CAT I, CAT II/III), its traffic density, its operating budget and its operating
environment all shape which fixtures, circuits, control philosophy and redundancy level actually make sense.

Specifying a full CAT III approach lighting system for a general aviation strip is as much a mismatch as
under-speccing a CCR bank for a busy international runway. Matching the AGL solution to the application is
where engineering judgement — not just a standards checklist — does the work.

## Explore AGL by Application

Nine ways AGL work is commissioned — by the kind of airport it serves, or the kind of project it is. Each
links to a dedicated page going deeper into that application's specific requirements, standards and
challenges.

### Commercial Airports

Full-service passenger airports handling scheduled traffic, typically ICAO Code C/D with standard runway and
taxiway lighting, PAPI, and redundant CCR configurations.

- Standard runway/taxiway edge, threshold & centreline systems

- Redundant CCR / changeover arrangements where the design calls for them

- Scheduled inspection & maintenance cycles

### International Airports

High-traffic hub airports operating in low-visibility conditions, often with CAT II/III precision approach
lighting, advanced monitoring and multi-runway coordination.

- CAT II/III approach lighting & stop bar systems

- SCADA-level monitoring & centralised control

- Compliance with ICAO Annex 14 and the national regulator's requirements

### Military Airfields

Combat and training airfields with operational requirements civilian standards don't fully address — rugged
fixtures, rapid-deployment options and covert or reduced-signature lighting modes.

- Ruggedised fixtures suited to the operating environment

- Covert / NVG-compatible lighting where required

- Rapid installation & mobile lighting kits

### Regional Airports

Smaller-scale, single-runway operations balancing regulatory compliance against tighter capital and operating
budgets.

- Simplified CCR & circuit configurations

- Right-sized PAPI & basic runway edge systems

- Budget-conscious design & phased upgrades

### General Aviation Airports

Small-aircraft airfields, often uncontrolled or lightly staffed, favouring low-cost, low-maintenance and
increasingly solar-powered lighting solutions.

- Low-intensity runway lighting (LIRL) systems

- Pilot-controlled lighting (PCL) options

- Solar & battery-powered fixtures for unstaffed strips

### Heliports

Helicopter-specific lighting geometry — perimeter and FATO/TLOF lighting, floodlighting and approach path
indicators — scaled to a fraction of a fixed-wing runway's footprint.

- FATO & TLOF perimeter and floodlighting where required

- Helicopter approach path indicator (HAPI)

- Rooftop & confined-area installation constraints

### Temporary & Emergency Airfield Lighting

Rapidly deployable lighting for rehabilitation works, emergency restoration and contingency airfields, where
speed of setup matters alongside photometric performance.

- Portable, battery- or generator-powered systems

- Quick-deploy kits sized to the mission

- Deployment in unprepared or damaged infrastructure

### Airport Runway Rehabilitation & Retrofit

Upgrading AGL infrastructure on a live or partially live runway — coordinating staged cutovers, temporary
lighting and outage windows around continuing operations.

- Phased cutover & staged commissioning planning

- Temporary lighting during works

- Coordination with NOTAMs & operational windows

### LED AGL Retrofit Projects

Converting incandescent and halogen fixtures to LED for energy savings and lower maintenance, while preserving
photometric compliance and CCR compatibility.

- CCR & series-circuit compatibility checks

- Post-retrofit photometric re-verification

- Energy-savings & lifecycle cost analysis

## How Application Shapes the AGL Solution

A high-level comparison of what typically drives the AGL scope for each application. Actual requirements
always depend on the specific aerodrome's category, regulator and operational profile.

Application | Typical Scale | Primary AGL Focus | Common Challenge

Commercial Airports | ICAO Code C/D, single–multi runway | Standard runway/taxiway systems, redundant CCRs | Balancing uptime with maintenance windows

International Airports | ICAO Code D/E, multi-runway hub | CAT II/III approach lighting, centralised monitoring | Low-visibility operations & strict compliance

Military Airfields | Varies — combat to training | Ruggedised, rapid-deploy, covert-mode fixtures | Non-standard operational & security requirements

Regional Airports | Single runway, moderate traffic | Right-sized, budget-conscious systems | Capital constraints vs compliance obligations

General Aviation Airports | Small aircraft, often uncontrolled | Low-intensity, pilot-controlled, solar lighting | Minimal staffing & power infrastructure

Heliports | FATO/TLOF, rooftop or ground-level | Perimeter, floodlighting & approach indicators | Confined footprint & installation access

Temporary/Emergency Lighting | Ad hoc, mission-driven | Portable, self-powered, rapid setup | Speed of deployment over permanence

Runway Rehabilitation & Retrofit | Existing live infrastructure | Staged cutover, temporary lighting | Maintaining operations during works

LED AGL Retrofit | Existing fixture base, any airport type | CCR compatibility, photometric re-verification | Proving compliance after conversion

### AGL Standards: ICAO Annex 14 Aerodrome Lighting, FAA, IEC

**Page summary:** AGL standards companion: ICAO Annex 14, FAA, DGCA India and BCAS aerodrome lighting requirements, testing standards and the ICAO vs FAA comparison.

# AGL Standards & Compliance Companion

ICAO Annex 14 • FAA AC • IEC • IS/BIS • DGCA

Practical interpretation of Airfield Ground Lighting standards, requirements, testing criteria and field
application — translated from regulatory language into engineering meaning you can use on the job.

DGCA CARs and applicable national regulations

ICAO Annex 14 / the applicable national adoption of it

ICAO Doc 9157 / FAA AC 150/5340 series

FAA AC 150/5345 series, IS/BIS, IEC

AAI / airport operator / EPC / consultant specification

TDS, installation manual, test certificate

An equipment specification (Level 4) is never the controlling aerodrome requirement — it implements Levels
1–3. Always check upward when in doubt.

Standard

Requirement

Practical Meaning

Field Application

L-824 Cable | FAA AC 150/5345-7F | High Voltage Spark + Insulation Resistance

L-823 Connectors | FAA AC 150/5345-26E | Style/Class qualification per AC 150/5345-53

Series Circuit (in-service) | IEC 61821:2011 | Periodic insulation & loop resistance

Signs (L-858) | FAA AC 150/5340-18H | Siting vs. holding-position markings

Stop Bars | ICAO Annex 14, Ch. 5 (9th Ed.) | Interlock functional test under fault condition

Runway Guard Lights | ICAO Annex 14, Ch. 5 (9th Ed.) | Flash rate & fixture configuration check

Obstacle Lights | ICAO Annex 14, Ch. 6 · FAA AC 150/5345-43 | Intensity class & flash synchronisation
