Circuit Selector Switch (L-847) | FAA AC 150/5345-5B | 10,000-cycle high-voltage switching test

### DGCA CAR Section 4, Series B, Part I — Aerodrome Design & Operations

India's national aerodrome design standard, issued under the Aircraft Rules, 1937

India's actual controlling aerodrome design requirement — not ICAO Annex 14 itself — substantially adopting
Annex 14, Volume I provisions (including AGL spacing, colour, siting and obstacle-lighting criteria) as
binding domestic requirements.

DGCA Civil Aviation Requirements, Section 4 – Aerodromes, Series B, Part I – Aerodrome Design & Operations
Issued under Rule 90 of the Aircraft Rules, 1937; a draft amendment covering definitions and apron ground-
handling criteria was issued 4 Oct 2025

Sets out India's national physical, visual-aid and electrical-system requirements for aerodrome design,
substantially mirroring ICAO Annex 14, Volume I provisions as binding domestic requirements enforceable by
DGCA.

For an Indian aerodrome project, this CAR — not Annex 14 directly — is the actual Level 1 controlling document
in the hierarchy above. Where India has filed a difference against an Annex 14 provision, the CAR text governs
domestically, not the ICAO text.

Confirm project compliance against the current CAR text and any open draft amendments rather than assuming
Annex 14 compliance alone satisfies DGCA requirements — cite the CAR paragraph, not just the Annex 14 clause,
in Indian compliance documentation.

### ICAO Annex 14 — Runway Edge Light Spacing

Volume I, Aerodrome Design and Operations

Edge lights sit no more than 60m apart — the ceiling that keeps the light row looking continuous to a pilot's
eye at approach speed.

ICAO Annex 14, Chapter 5 — Visual Aids for Navigation Clause reference: verify exact numbering against the 9th
Edition (numbering has shifted across recent editions)

Runway edge lights shall be spaced at intervals of not more than 60m.

The 60m ceiling sets the maximum gap a pilot's eye will see between light points at typical approach speeds —
closer spacing is permitted, wider is not.

Verify spacing during design review and again at as-built survey; a common installation error is exceeding
spacing on curved or non-standard-length runways.

### ICAO Annex 14 — Runway Edge Light Colour

Volume I, Aerodrome Design and Operations

Yellow caution zone begins in the last 600m or one-third of runway length, whichever is less — the rest stays
variable white.

ICAO Annex 14, Chapter 5 — Visual Aids for Navigation Clause reference: verify exact numbering against the 9th
Edition (numbering has shifted across recent editions)

Edge lights shall show variable white, except in the last 600m or one-third of runway length, where yellow is
used.

The yellow caution zone gives pilots an unambiguous visual cue that remaining runway is limited, independent
of any distance markings.

Confirm the yellow/white transition point is measured correctly against actual runway length, not the declared
distances, during commissioning.

### FAA AC 150/5345-10H — Constant Current Regulators & Regulator Monitors

Constant Current Regulator equipment specification

The current FAA CCR/regulator-monitor spec — qualification testing includes humidity cycling (five 48-hour
cycles at up to 55°C) followed by CCR input voltage tests, in addition to output regulation accuracy.

FAA AC 150/5345-10H, Specification for Constant Current Regulators and Regulator Monitors Revision H — Table 1
updated for CCR conformance testing; para 3.3.2 updated on maximum operating point

Output current must be held within the tolerance specified in Chapter 3 across the full connected load range,
and the CCR/monitor assembly must pass the Chapter 4 qualification tests, including environmental cycling (5 ×
48-hour humidity cycles, max chamber temp 131°F/55°C) followed by input voltage testing per para 4.2.1.1.

The humidity-cycling requirement exists because CCR cabinets sit in outdoor equipment enclosures for decades —
a unit that only passes a bench test at room conditions can still fail in the field from condensation-driven
insulation breakdown.

When reviewing a CCR type-test report, confirm it references revision H specifically (not the superseded 2010
edition) and that the humidity-cycling sequence is documented as five distinct 48-hour cycles, not a single
extended soak.

### FAA AC 150/5345-47C — Series to Series Isolation Transformers

L-830 (60Hz) / L-831 (50Hz) isolation transformer specification

Covers L-830 (60Hz) and L-831 (50Hz) series isolation transformers, encapsulated in a watertight case;
transformers must withstand a specified hi-pot test between primary and secondary windings (confirm exact test
voltage/duration against your copy).

FAA AC 150/5345-47C, Specification for Series to Series Isolation Transformers for Airport Lighting Systems
Cancels AC 150/5345-47B, dated 30 Jun 2005

Transformers are designated Type L-830 (60Hz operation) or L-831 (50Hz operation), with a numerical suffix
identifying wattage/current rating per Table 1. They must consist of electrically separate primary and
secondary coils wound on a core, encapsulated in a watertight case with rubber (or equivalent) connectors, and
must withstand a specified high-potential (hi-pot) test between primary and secondary windings without
breakdown.

The 50Hz/60Hz split (L-831 vs L-830) matters directly for Indian and most non-North-American projects —
specifying the wrong frequency designation on a BOQ is a straightforward but real procurement error, distinct
from the wattage/current suffix.

Hi-pot testing should be part of incoming goods inspection, not assumed from the manufacturer's factory test
certificate alone; also confirm the L-830/L-831 frequency designation matches the project's supply frequency
before ordering, not just the wattage rating.

### IEC 61822:2009 — Constant Current Regulators (Superseded)

Electrical installations for lighting and beaconing of aerodromes — CCR requirements

IEC 61822:2009 specified requirements for a 6.6A constant current regulator for aeronautical ground lighting
series circuits. It has been withdrawn and replaced — see IEC 61820-3-2:2023 below.

IEC 61822:2009, Electrical installations for lighting and beaconing of aerodromes — Constant current
regulators Second edition, cancelled and replaced the 2002 first edition

Specified requirements for a Constant Current Regulator with a nominal output of 6.6A for use in an
aeronautical ground lighting constant-current series circuit.

This was the reference CCR spec for series-circuit AGL systems for over a decade. It did not cover power-
electronic converter systems or LED-driven AGL architectures.

Do not specify or reference IEC 61822 as the current standard on new tenders or drawings — it has been
cancelled and replaced. Retained here for historical/legacy-installation reference only.

### IEC 61820-3-2:2023 — Power Supplies for AGL Series Circuits

Current CCR / power electronic converter system (PECS) standard

Current IEC standard for power electronic converter systems (PECS), including 6.6A CCR setups, powering AGL
series circuits. Replaces IEC 61822:2009.

IEC 61820-3-2:2023, Electrical installations for lighting and beaconing of aerodromes — Part 3-2: Requirements
for power supplies — Particular requirements for series circuits First edition, cancels and replaces IEC
61822:2009

Specifies requirements for power electronic converter systems (PECS) dedicated to powering AGL circuits with
series-circuit topology — including updated 6.6A CCR requirements and new requirements for general PECS,
including LED-based luminaire systems.

Widens the scope beyond the traditional 6.6A CCR to cover modern power-electronic supplies for LED-based
series circuits, while still allowing conventional CCR configurations. Safety requirements now reference IEC
62477-1/-2.

Use this as the current reference for any new CCR or PECS procurement or type-test review; treat an IEC 61822
test certificate on new equipment as a flag to ask for re-verification against IEC 61820-3-2.

### IEC 61820/61821/61823/62144 — AGL Electrical Series Family

Map of the wider IEC aerodrome electrical-installation series

Beyond the CCR-focused 61822/61820-3-2, the wider IEC 618xx family covers system design, maintenance, series
transformers, and control/monitoring — useful as a map before you go looking for the wrong part.

IEC 61820 family, Electrical installations for lighting and beaconing of aerodromes Family list per ICAO Doc
9157, Aerodrome Design Manual, Part 5

IEC 61820: system design and installation requirements for constant-current series circuits · IEC 61821:
maintenance of AGL circuits and equipment · IEC 61823: AGL series transformers · IEC 62144: technical
requirements for AGL control and monitoring systems · IEC 62294: connecting devices · IEC TS 61827:
characteristics of inset and elevated fixtures.

The family is split by function, not by component — so a transformer question sits in 61823 while its
installation sits in 61820 and its maintenance sits in 61821. Don't expect one document to cover a component
end-to-end.

Use this as a lookup table when a spec calls out "IEC 618xx" generically — confirm which specific part number
the requirement actually needs before searching for it.

### ICAO Annex 14 — PAPI Siting Criteria

Visual glide slope indicator systems

PAPI glide-path angle is fixed by obstacle-clearance math, not by eye — any change to the approach area forces
a re-calculation, not just a flight check.

ICAO Annex 14, Chapter 5 and Doc 9157 Aerodrome Design Manual, Part 4 Clause reference: verify exact numbering
against the 9th Edition (numbering has shifted across recent editions)

PAPI units must be sited such that the indicated glide path clears all obstacles in the approach area by a
specified margin.

The glide path angle isn't just an aiming preference — it's derived from obstacle clearance calculations
specific to that runway's approach surface.

Any change to approach-area terrain or structures after PAPI commissioning requires a re-verification of the
siting calculation, not just a flight check.

### FAA AC 150/5340-30J — Design & Installation Details for Airport Visual Aids

Master installation-detail AC for AGL systems

The consolidated FAA installation-detail AC for runway/taxiway edge lighting, centerline and TDZ lighting,
approach lighting, PAPI, signs, wind cones, beacons and obstruction lights.

FAA AC 150/5340-30J, Design and Installation Details for Airport Visual Aids Cancels and replaces AC
150/5340-30H (2014)

Use of this AC is not mandatory in general, but it is mandatory for projects funded through the Airport
Improvement Program (AIP) or Passenger Facility Charges (PFC). Configurations in the AC are an accepted means
of meeting the visual-aid requirements of 14 CFR Part 139.311.

It is the single largest source of installation drawings and construction detail for U.S. AGL work —
foundations, mounting, frangibility, cable routing and transformer/base installation are all covered here
rather than in the equipment ACs.

Confirm which funding source applies to a given project before treating this AC as optional — federally funded
work must follow it, and its detail drawings are the usual installation reference regardless.

### ICAO Annex 14 — Runway Threshold & Wing Bar Lights

Volume I, Aerodrome Design and Operations

Green, one-way lights mark exactly where the usable runway begins — and must move with the threshold if it's
ever displaced.

ICAO Annex 14, Chapter 5 — Visual Aids for Navigation Clause reference: verify exact numbering against the 9th
Edition (numbering has shifted across recent editions)

Threshold lights are unidirectional, fixed, green lights arranged across the runway at the threshold; wing bar
lights extend the row laterally where additional threshold conspicuity is needed.

Green is reserved for "start of usable runway" only, distinguishing it unambiguously from edge (white/yellow),
end (red) and taxiway (blue/green) colour coding.

Where the threshold is displaced, confirm the lights are physically relocated with it, not left at the
original pavement threshold — a common as-built discrepancy.

### ICAO Annex 14 — Runway End Lights

Volume I, Aerodrome Design and Operations

Red, one-way lights mark the far end of the runway for an aircraft already on it — the mirror image of the
green threshold lights.

ICAO Annex 14, Chapter 5 — Visual Aids for Navigation Clause reference: verify exact numbering against the 9th
Edition (numbering has shifted across recent editions)

Runway end lights are unidirectional, fixed, red lights showing toward the runway, marking the extremity of
the runway for an aircraft on the runway.

Where a fitting combines threshold and end functions (bidirectional green/red), the two colours must be
correctly oriented — green faces approaching traffic, red faces the runway.

On commissioning, walk the runway end at night and confirm no white or green leakage is visible from the
runway side of a combined threshold/end fitting.

### ICAO Annex 14 — Runway Centre Line Lights

Volume I, Aerodrome Design and Operations

Colour shifts from white toward red as the runway end approaches, giving a pilot a built-in countdown of
remaining runway on CAT II/III approaches.

ICAO Annex 14, Chapter 5 — Visual Aids for Navigation Clause reference: verify exact numbering against the 9th
Edition (numbering has shifted across recent editions)

Runway centre line lights are inset, fixed lights on or near the runway centre line, required for CAT II/III
and certain other precision-approach runways, with colour transitioning from white toward the far end to
indicate remaining runway length.

Because they're inset and walked/rolled over directly by aircraft, they carry the heaviest mechanical and
photometric duty of any AGL fixture on the runway.

Inset centreline fixtures are the most common casualty of resurfacing work — confirm reinstatement position
and level tolerance against the design survey, not just visual alignment.

### ICAO Annex 14 — Touchdown Zone Lights

Volume I, Aerodrome Design and Operations

White barrettes run 900m from the threshold or to the runway midpoint — whichever is shorter, so short runways
get proportionally less coverage.

ICAO Annex 14, Chapter 5 — Visual Aids for Navigation Clause reference: verify exact numbering against the 9th
Edition (numbering has shifted across recent editions)

Touchdown zone lights must be provided on runways available for low-visibility use, to give enhanced
identification of the touchdown area. The lighting extends from the landing threshold for 900m or to the
runway midpoint, whichever is the least.

The 900m/midpoint rule means shorter runways get proportionally less TDZ coverage — don't assume every CAT-
capable runway carries a full 900m of barrettes.

Check the actual runway length against the 900m/midpoint rule during design before assuming a fixed barrette
count; the terminating barrette pair position is a common design-review omission.

### ICAO Annex 14 — Taxiway Centre Line Lights

Volume I, Aerodrome Design and Operations

Green inset lights that pull in tighter on curves and change treatment specifically where they cross a runway.

ICAO Annex 14, Chapter 5 — Visual Aids for Navigation Clause reference: verify exact numbering against the 9th
Edition (numbering has shifted across recent editions)

Taxiway centre line lights are green, inset lights on or near the taxiway centre line, with reduced spacing on
curves and specific treatment where a taxiway centre line intersects a runway.

Tighter spacing on curves compensates for the shorter visual "look-ahead" a pilot has when the fixture line is
bending away from straight-line sightlines.

Verify curve spacing separately from straight-section spacing during design review — applying straight-section
spacing on curves is a recurring design error.

### ICAO Annex 14 — Taxiway Edge Lights

Volume I, Aerodrome Design and Operations

Blue elevated lights mark the lateral limits of a taxiway — the one colour in the AGL palette reserved
exclusively for this job.

ICAO Annex 14, Chapter 5 — Visual Aids for Navigation Clause reference: verify exact numbering against the 9th
Edition (numbering has shifted across recent editions)

Taxiway edge lights are blue, elevated lights along the edges of a taxiway, apron or holding bay, used where
taxiway centre line lighting is not provided or is insufficient on its own.

Blue is otherwise unused elsewhere in the AGL colour scheme, so it reads unambiguously as "taxiway boundary"
even in mixed runway/taxiway/apron lighting environments.

Elevated edge fittings on taxiways are frangibility-critical — confirm frangible mounting is used and that the
fitting hasn't been substituted with a non-frangible base during a later maintenance replacement.

### ICAO Annex 14 — Stop Bars

Volume I, Aerodrome Design and Operations

Red lights across the taxiway that must never be lit at the same moment as the centre line lights beyond them
— the interlock is the safety-critical part.

ICAO Annex 14, Chapter 5 — Visual Aids for Navigation Clause reference: verify exact numbering against the 9th
Edition (numbering has shifted across recent editions)

Stop bars are unidirectional red lights installed across a taxiway at a runway-holding position, with
provision for selective switching and, where used for low-visibility operations, interlocking with the taxiway
centre line lights beyond them.

The interlock is the safety-critical part — it should not be physically possible to have a stop bar lit while
the centre line lights immediately beyond it are also lit, or vice versa in the intended sequence.

Interlock logic must be functionally tested at commissioning under simulated fault conditions (e.g., a fixture
failure), not just under normal switching — this is one of the highest-consequence AGL control tests.

### ICAO Annex 14 — Runway Guard Lights

Volume I, Aerodrome Design and Operations

Yellow flashing lights at the holding position — a visual warning cue, not a physical interlock like a stop
bar.

ICAO Annex 14, Chapter 5 — Visual Aids for Navigation Clause reference: verify exact numbering against the 9th
Edition (numbering has shifted across recent editions)

Runway guard lights are yellow flashing lights installed at a runway-holding position, in one of two
configurations, to give an alerting indication of approach to a runway.

They're a warning cue rather than a control device — unlike a stop bar, they don't physically or logically
interlock with runway occupancy, they just make the holding position conspicuous.

Confirm flash rate and light configuration match the elevated or inset fitting standard being used — mixing
configurations across the same airfield creates inconsistent pilot cues.

### IS 12290:1987 — Isolating Transformers for Airport Lighting

Bureau of Indian Standards, Electrotechnical Division (ETD 24)

India's core specification for series isolating transformers used in airport lighting — covers construction,
electrical ratings, insulation resistance and the 20-cycle endurance test.

IS 12290:1987, Specification for Isolating Transformers for Airport Lighting Systems Prepared with reference
to FAA AC 150/5345-47 (1975 edition), per its own foreword

Sets construction, rating and testing requirements for series isolating transformers, including minimum
insulation resistance (measured at specified DC test voltages, clauses 5.5.1/5.5.3) and a 20-cycle test
(clause 5.5.2) simulating repeated energisation cycles.

The 20-cycle test is the distinguishing feature versus a one-off hi-pot check — it's meant to catch insulation
or connector weaknesses that only show up after repeated thermal/electrical cycling, closer to real field
duty.

When reviewing a manufacturer's IS 12290 test certificate, confirm it actually reports the 20-cycle result and
both primary/secondary insulation resistance values — a certificate that only shows a single hi-pot pass/fail
is incomplete against this standard.

### FAA AC 150/5345-26E — L-823 Plug & Receptacle Cable Connectors

Series-circuit connector specification

Covers the L-823 plug/receptacle connectors used on underground power cable, isolation transformer leads and
light fixture leads — voluntary in general, mandatory for AIP/PFC-funded projects.

FAA AC 150/5345-26E, Specification for L-823 Plug and Receptacle, Cable Connectors Issued 16 Dec 2021, cancels
AC 150/5345-26D (30 Sep 2008)

Specifies plug-and-receptacle connectors for underground power cables, isolation transformer leads and light
fixture leads, identified by style number (e.g. "L-823, Style 3"); Class A connectors must be supplied with
protective caps unless the buyer requests otherwise. Qualified products are listed under AC 150/5345-53, the
Airport Lighting Equipment Certification Program.

The style number is the actual ordering/compliance reference on drawings and BOQs — "L-823 connector" alone is
not specific enough; the style governs conductor size, pin/socket configuration and application (primary
series circuit vs. transformer lead vs. fixture lead).

When checking a connector delivery against a tender BOQ, confirm the style number on the datasheet matches the
drawing call-out, and check the product against the current AC 150/5345-53 qualified-products list rather than
trusting a general "L-823 compliant" claim.

### FAA AC 150/5345-7F — L-824 Underground Electrical Cable

Airport lighting circuit cable specification

Specifies L-824 series-circuit cable (Type B EPR or Type C XLPE insulation, 5,000V, non-shielded, single-
conductor 7-strand), with production testing anchored on High Voltage Spark and Insulation Resistance per ICEA
T-26-465/NEMA WC54.

FAA AC 150/5345-7F, Specification for L-824 Underground Electrical Cable for Airport Lighting Circuits
Effective 6 months after issue; only cable qualified to this AC is listed under AC 150/5345-53

L-824 primary series-circuit conductors are single-conductor, seven-strand, rated 5,000V, non-shielded, with
either Type B (ethylene propylene rubber) or Type C (cross-linked polyethylene) insulation. Qualification
testing (§4.1.2) and ongoing production testing — at minimum High Voltage Spark and Insulation Resistance, per
ICEA T-26-465/NEMA WC54 frequency — are both required; the manufacturer must maintain an ISO 9001-equivalent
quality program (§4.1.3).

Because this is series-circuit cable carrying up to several thousand volts at fault, insulation type and rated
voltage aren't interchangeable with general-purpose power cable of the same gauge — Type B vs Type C affects
flexibility and temperature performance, which matters for cold-climate or high-cycle installations.

Request the manufacturer's most recent production test report (High Voltage Spark + Insulation Resistance) on
the actual reel/batch being supplied, not just a type-test certificate from qualification — §4.1.4 requires
the manufacturer to make current production records available on request.

### FAA AC 150/5345-28H — L-880/L-881 PAPI Systems

Precision Approach Path Indicator equipment specification

Covers the L-880 (4-unit) and L-881 (2-unit, abbreviated) PAPI light housing assemblies — remote on/off
control, two selectable night-mode intensity settings, and automatic fail-to-night-mode behaviour on photocell
failure.

FAA AC 150/5345-28H, Precision Approach Path Indicator (PAPI) Systems Cancels AC 150/5345-28G;
siting/installation content now lives separately in AC 150/5340-30

Specifies the L-880 (four light-housing-assembly) and L-881 (two-LHA, abbreviated) PAPI configurations, in
Style A (voltage-powered, power and control unit) or Style B (current-driven, 6.6A series circuit) versions.
The unit must offer remote on/off control, two selectable night-mode intensities (approx. 5% and 20% of day-
mode), and must automatically revert to night mode if the photoelectric control fails.

Style A vs Style B is a power-architecture decision, not a cosmetic one — Style B rides the same 6.6A series
circuit as the runway edge lights, while Style A needs its own constant-voltage feed and PCU; mixing the wrong
style into an existing circuit design is a common tender-stage error.

During commissioning, verify the automatic fail-to-night-mode behaviour by disabling the photocell input and
confirming intensity drops rather than staying at day-mode or lamp failure — this is a safety-relevant
behaviour, not just a housekeeping feature.

### FAA AC 150/5345-46F — Runway, Taxiway, Heliport & Vertiport Light Fixtures

In-pavement and elevated light fixture specification

The current FAA fixture spec — extended in this revision to cover heliport and vertiport fixtures alongside
runway/taxiway types; retains the mandatory yield-point/frangibility requirement (150 ft-lb bending moment)
common to elevated fixtures.

FAA AC 150/5345-46F, Specification for Runway, Taxiway, Heliport, and Vertiport Light Fixtures Cancels AC
150/5345-46E (issued 2 Mar 2016); scope widened from "Runway and Taxiway" to include heliport/vertiport
fixtures

Each elevated light fixture must have a yield point that separates cleanly before any other part of the
fixture is damaged, and must withstand a bending moment of 150 ft-lb (203 N·m) without failure. Photometric
axes are defined relative to the installed fixture (horizontal axis parallel to runway centreline), and every
type/class/mode/option/style combination must undergo qualification testing per Chapter 4, including
photometric measurement across different lamp manufacturers, wattages and lens combinations.

The yield-point requirement is the frangibility mechanism that lets an elevated fixture break away under
aircraft/vehicle impact without becoming a secondary hazard — it's a safety requirement, not just a mechanical
nicety, and it's specific to elevated (not in-pavement) fixtures.

When a legacy fixture was qualified under AC 150/5345-46E, confirm whether it needs re-qualification under
-46F before use on a new AIP/PFC-funded project — check the current AC 150/5345-53 qualified-products list
rather than assuming carryover.

### FAA AC 150/5345-42K — Light Bases, Transformer Housings & Junction Boxes

L-867/L-868 base and accessory specification

Governs the L-867 (base-mounted) and L-868 (in-pavement) light bases, transformer housings, junction boxes,
and elevated light covers/stakes — sizing, load rating, and dissimilar-metal corrosion control.

FAA AC 150/5345-42K, Specification for Airport Light Bases, Transformer Housings, Junction Boxes, and
Accessories Cancels AC 150/5345-42J, dated 12 Sep 2019

Type L-867 serves as a mounting base for elevated fixtures, a transformer housing, and an electrical junction
box, and must withstand occasional light vehicular loading. Bases and extensions are assigned Class
(material/finish) and Size (nominal diameter) designations — e.g. a 12-inch L-868 base is designated "L-868E."
Separation material between dissimilar metals (flange rings, spacer rings) must not deform under 450 psi, to
prevent galvanic action and bolt loosening over time.

The dissimilar-metal / galvanic-action clause is easy to overlook on a BOQ but shows up years later as bolt
seizure or base corrosion at the flange — it's the reason a "like-for-like" base swap during maintenance can
still fail if the wrong hardware finish is substituted.

Confirm the base type/size designation on delivered hardware (e.g. "L-868E") matches the drawing call-out
before installation, and check that separation material is actually present at flange joints during a
maintenance base swap, not just at initial construction.

### FAA AC 150/5345-44 — Runway & Taxiway Signs

L-858 lighted and unlighted sign specification

Covers the six FAA sign types (L-858Y/R/L etc.) used on runways and taxiways, in five sizes, five styles and
two classes — power must reach signs only through breakaway connectors within the frangible point, never via
above-ground cable.

FAA AC 150/5345-44, Specification for Runway and Taxiway Signs The FAA's own AC index has shown this
specification transitioning between revisions; confirm the current issued edition before use

Six sign types are specified (mandatory instruction, location, direction, destination, runway distance-
remaining, and taxiway ending marker), across five sizes and two classes. Power to a sign must be delivered
through breakaway cable connectors installed within the frangible point — there must be no above-ground power
cable connections directly to a sign.

The breakaway-connector-within-the-frangible-point rule exists so that if a sign is struck, the electrical
connection separates at the same moment as the mechanical structure — a sign that stays "live" after being
knocked over is a hazard the frangibility requirement is specifically meant to prevent.

During installation inspection, trace the power feed into each sign and confirm the disconnect point sits
within the frangible coupling, not spliced above grade — this is a common shortcut on retrofit sign
replacements.

### ICAO Annex 14 — Obstacle Lighting

Volume I, Aerodrome Design and Operations

Object height and background decide low/medium/high-intensity class — steady red for night, flashing white for
daytime conspicuity on tall structures.

ICAO Annex 14, Chapter 6 — Visual Aids for Denoting Obstacles Clause reference: verify exact numbering against
the 9th Edition (numbering has shifted across recent editions)

Objects that need to be marked as obstacles are indicated by obstacle lights, obstacle markings, or both,
unless their shape or function makes lighting alone sufficient (e.g. an illuminated structure). Obstacle
lights are classed as low, medium or high intensity (Type A/B/C etc.), selected according to the object's
height and the surrounding background — steady red for low/medium intensity, flashing white for high-intensity
daytime marking of very tall structures.

The intensity/colour selection isn't purely aesthetic — a flashing high-intensity white light on a tall mast
is chosen specifically for daytime conspicuity against sky background, while steady red is calibrated for
night-time visibility without dazzling pilots; substituting one class for another defeats the purpose the
height calculation was based on.

Cross-check obstacle light class selection against the actual measured object height and its obstacle
limitation surface penetration at design stage, and confirm during commissioning that flash characteristics
(rate, synchronisation across multiple lights on the same structure) are set as specified — unsynchronised
flashing on a multi-light structure is a common field defect.

### ICAO Annex 14 — Approach Lighting Systems (ALS)

Volume I, Aerodrome Design and Operations

Light-bar length and configuration scale directly with the runway's approach category, from a simple SALS row
up to a full CAT II/III system with crossbars.

ICAO Annex 14, Chapter 5 — Visual Aids for Navigation Clause reference: verify exact numbering against the 9th
Edition (numbering has shifted across recent editions)

An approach lighting system provides a row of light bars, and where applicable cross bars, along the extended
centre line of a runway to guide the pilot during the final approach. The configuration, total length and
light intensity scale up from a Simple Approach Lighting System (SALS) for non-precision/lower-category
operations to a full precision approach lighting system for Category II/III operations, which is longer and
adds centreline and crossbar barrettes.

The ALS category isn't a design choice made in isolation — it follows directly from the runway's
declared/approved approach classification (non-precision, CAT I, CAT II/III), so a design review should start
from that classification rather than working backward from a preferred layout.

Verify light bar spacing and total approach lighting length against the specific system type before
construction, and confirm frangibility and elevated/inset mounting requirements for any structure within the
approach light plane.

### FAA AC 150/5345-53D — Airport Lighting Equipment Certification Program

Qualification framework (ALECP) for L-series AGL equipment

Sets out the process by which L-series AGL equipment — fixtures, CCRs, isolating transformers, cable,
connectors, signs — is qualified through FAA-recognized independent testing laboratories and placed on the
Qualified Products List (QPL) before it can be specified on AIP/PFC-funded work (summary — verify current
revision against FAA's ALECP guidance).

FAA AC 150/5345-53, Airport Lighting Equipment Certification Program Confirm current revision letter — this AC
has been updated multiple times

Establishes the qualification pathway equipment manufacturers must follow — testing by an FAA-recognized
independent laboratory against the relevant individual AC 150/5345-series specification — before a product can
appear on the FAA's Qualified Products List (QPL) for that equipment class.

A manufacturer's own type-test report is not, by itself, equivalent to QPL listing — the independent-lab step
is what makes the qualification acceptable for federally funded work, and a project spec calling for "FAA-
approved" equipment of this class typically means QPL-listed.

Before accepting an equipment submittal, check the current FAA QPL for that item rather than relying solely on
the vendor's test certificate, and confirm the QPL entry matches the exact model/part number being supplied,
not just the product family.

### FAA AC 150/5340-18H — Standards for Airport Sign Systems

Siting, sizing and legend design for L-858 sign systems

Covers where signs go and what they say — mandatory instruction signs, location signs, direction signs and
runway distance-remaining signs — as distinct from AC 150/5345-44, which specifies the L-858 sign hardware
itself.

FAA AC 150/5340-18H, Standards for Airport Sign Systems Companion document to the L-858 equipment spec, AC
150/5345-44; cancels AC 150/5340-18G, dated 10 May 2019

Defines sign types (mandatory instruction, location, direction, destination, information, runway distance-
remaining), their required siting relative to taxiway/runway edges and holding positions, and legend
format/sizing appropriate to the airport's reference code.

The equipment spec defines what a compliant sign is built like; this AC defines where it has to stand and what
it has to say — a fully compliant L-858 fixture in the wrong location or with the wrong legend still fails the
requirement.

Cross-check sign siting and legend content against this AC during design review, separately from confirming
the physical sign itself is a QPL-listed L-858 product under AC 150/5345-44 and the ALECP. If you're holding
an older -18F or -18G copy, note this AC has moved on twice since (18F → 18G in 2019, 18G → 18H in 2024).

### IEC 61821:2011 — Maintenance of Aeronautical Ground Lighting

In-service maintenance and functional testing of AGL series circuits

Sets out recommended maintenance activities and in-service functional/electrical testing for constant-current
series circuits and their associated CCRs, isolating transformers and fixtures, complementing the
design/equipment standards in the 61820 family (summary — verify current edition and exact test intervals
against the source document).

IEC 61821, Electrical installations for lighting and beaconing of aerodromes — Maintenance of aeronautical
ground lighting Part of the wider IEC 618xx family — confirm current edition

Covers routine and periodic maintenance activities for AGL series-circuit installations, including insulation
resistance checks, loop resistance testing, isolating transformer condition checks, and CCR output
verification, intended to detect degradation before it causes an in-service failure.

The design standards (IEC 61820 / 61820-3-2) set what a new installation must achieve; this standard is what
keeps an installation performing to the same margins years after commissioning — insulation resistance in
particular degrades gradually and needs a recurring check, not a one-time pass.

Build a periodic maintenance test schedule — insulation resistance, loop resistance, CCR output — directly
from this standard's referenced test methods rather than an ad-hoc interval, and log trend data over time
rather than only recording pass/fail against a single threshold.

### ICAO Annex 14 — Aerodrome Beacon

Volume I, Aerodrome Design and Operations

Alternating white/green flashes mark the aerodrome's location for aircraft in flight — a location aid, not a
runway or approach cue.

ICAO Annex 14, Chapter 5 — Visual Aids for Navigation Clause reference: verify exact numbering against the 9th
Edition (numbering has shifted across recent editions)

An aerodrome beacon is provided at an aerodrome intended for use at night when specified by the appropriate
authority, typically where visual identification of the aerodrome from the air is otherwise difficult; a land
aerodrome beacon shows alternating white and green flashes.

The beacon is a location aid, not an approach or runway-alignment aid — it tells a pilot where the aerodrome
is, not which runway or approach path to fly, and shouldn't be confused with approach or runway lighting
during a design review.

Confirm beacon siting doesn't create a line-of-sight or glare conflict with the control tower or nearby
approach paths, and that flash colour/rate is verified during commissioning against the current edition's
figures.

### FAA AC 150/5345-43 — Obstruction Lighting Equipment

L-810/L-864/L-865/L-856 obstruction light specification

Covers low-intensity (L-810), medium-intensity (L-864/L-865) and high-intensity (L-856) obstruction light
equipment used to mark structures and terrain penetrating obstacle limitation surfaces (summary — verify exact
light-type table and photometric figures in the current edition).

FAA AC 150/5345-43, Specification for Obstruction Lighting Equipment Confirm current revision letter before
referencing test tables

Each obstruction light type — L-810 low-intensity steady red, L-864/L-865 medium-intensity white/red, L-856
high-intensity white — has its own photometric intensity, flash-rate and colour requirements, and equipment
must pass the AC's environmental and photometric qualification tests before appearing on an FAA-approved
equipment list.

Choosing the wrong light type for a given structure is a design error, not just an equipment substitution —
the AC ties light-type selection to obstruction height and surrounding lighting environment, so swapping a
medium-intensity fixture for a low-intensity one changes conspicuity, not just cost.

When reviewing an obstruction-light submittal, confirm the fixture's FAA-approved equipment list entry
corresponds to the specific light type called for in the design, not a generic "obstruction light"
description.

### FAA AC 150/5345-51 — Discharge-Type Flashing Light Equipment

Condenser-discharge (strobe) sequenced flasher units for approach lighting

Covers the condenser-discharge ("strobe") flashing light units used in sequenced flashing lead-in lights on
approach lighting systems, including flash intensity and firing-sequence timing (summary — verify exact timing
tolerances in the current edition).

FAA AC 150/5345-51, Specification for Discharge-Type Flashing Light Equipment Verify current revision and
timing-tolerance tables

Flasher units must meet specified peak flash intensity and pulse-duration limits, and where used in a
sequenced flashing system, individual units must fire in the correct order within tolerance so the sequence
reads as a single moving light along the approach lighting system.

The firing-sequence tolerance is what makes a sequenced flasher system look like a single ball of light
"running" toward the runway rather than a scatter of independent flashes — a unit firing outside tolerance
breaks that visual effect even with correct individual flash intensity.

During commissioning, verify sequence timing end-to-end along the ALS rather than at each flasher head in
isolation, since one mistimed unit disrupts the perceived motion for an approaching pilot.

### FAA AC 150/5345-13 — L-841 Auxiliary Relay Cabinet Assembly

Series-circuit selection/isolation relay cabinet specification

Covers the L-841 relay cabinet used to switch or isolate sections of a series AGL circuit downstream of a CCR
— for example, selectively energizing a taxiway lead-in section (summary — verify current relay-rating tables
in the current edition).

FAA AC 150/5345-13, Specification for L-841 Auxiliary Relay Cabinet Assembly Verify current revision and relay
contact rating tables

The relay cabinet's contactors/relays must be rated for the full series-circuit current and voltage they
switch, and the cabinet must provide monitoring/feedback contacts so relay position can be confirmed at the
airfield lighting control system.

An L-841 cabinet lets one CCR feed multiple circuit sections without a separate regulator per section, but
only if the relay contacts are rated for the full series current — undersized contacts on a switched circuit
section are a known field failure point.

Confirm relay contact ratings match the CCR output current on the circuit being switched, and that position-
feedback contacts are wired back to the lighting control panel so control-room indications reflect actual
relay state.

### ICAO Annex 14 — Mandatory Instruction & Guidance Signs

Volume I, Aerodrome Design and Operations

Red background with white legend means stop-and-clear; the complementary yellow/black scheme is wayfinding
only.

ICAO Annex 14, Chapter 5 — Visual Aids for Navigation Clause reference: verify exact numbering against the 9th
Edition (numbering has shifted across recent editions)

Mandatory instruction signs use a red background with white inscription and mark locations such as runway-
holding positions, no-entry points and other restrictions requiring clearance; other aeronautical ground signs
(direction, location, destination) use the complementary yellow/black colour scheme and support wayfinding
rather than restriction.

The red/white versus yellow/black split is the pilot's fastest visual cue for "stop/restricted" versus
"informational" — mixing up sign colour and function during design or replacement undermines exactly the cue
the standard is meant to create.

During a taxiway/apron lighting design review, cross-check every mandatory instruction sign location against
current runway-holding position markings; a sign relocated without an updated marking survey is a common as-
built discrepancy.

### ICAO Annex 14 — Illuminated Wind Direction Indicator

Volume I, Aerodrome Design and Operations

Sited for unobstructed airflow from every likely wind direction, not just the prevailing one — and illuminated
wherever night operations occur.

ICAO Annex 14, Chapter 5 — Visual Aids for Navigation Clause reference: verify exact numbering against the 9th
Edition (numbering has shifted across recent editions)

A wind direction indicator (wind cone/sock) shall be located so its indications are not disturbed by nearby
objects and remain visible from aircraft in flight or moving on the aerodrome; where night operations occur,
the indicator must be illuminated so wind direction stays visible in low light.

Because the indicator's usefulness depends on unobstructed airflow reaching it, siting is as much a part of
compliance as the fixture itself — an illuminated wind cone placed in the wind shadow of a building or tree
line can meet the lighting requirement while still failing its underlying purpose.

When siting or relocating a wind cone, check upwind obstacle clearance from all likely wind directions, not
just the prevailing one, and confirm illumination stays visible against apron floodlighting at night.

### IEC 61823 — Aeronautical Beacons

Photometric & mechanical characteristics of aerodrome/identification beacons

Specifies photometric (intensity, flash characteristics) and mechanical requirements for aerodrome and
identification beacons, complementing ICAO Annex 14's provision criteria with testable equipment parameters
(summary — verify exact photometric tables in the current edition).

IEC 61823, Aeronautical ground lighting — Characteristics of aeronautical beacons Verify current edition and
photometric tables

Beacon equipment must meet specified minimum light intensity and flash-rate values for its category (aerodrome
beacon, identification beacon), verified by photometric test, in addition to mechanical/environmental
durability requirements for outdoor rotating or flashing beacon assemblies.

ICAO Annex 14 sets out when and where a beacon is required and what colour/flash pattern it should show; IEC
61823 is the equipment-side standard that lets a manufacturer's beacon be tested and shown to meet those
photometric figures — the two standards work together rather than one replacing the other.

When reviewing a beacon type-test certificate, confirm it references IEC 61823 photometric results
specifically, not just a general ingress-protection or mechanical rating, since intensity/flash-rate
compliance is the parameter Annex 14's siting criteria assume is already met.

### FAA AC 150/5345-56B — L-890 Airport Lighting Control & Monitoring System (ALCMS)

ALCMS equipment specification — centralized control & monitoring of lighted visual aids

The PLC-based system that centralizes switching and status monitoring of AGL circuits; the AC defines four
escalating monitoring tiers (Type A through Type D), with Type D — individual lamp-out monitoring — reserved
for CAT III / SMGCS-equipped airports.

FAA AC 150/5345-56B, Specification for L-890 Airport Lighting Control and Monitoring System (ALCMS) Revision
B, 29 Sep 2011 — supersedes the 2004 edition; adds a monitoring-variance notification note at Table 8

Defines the minimum requirements for a PLC-based ALCMS that centralizes control and monitoring of lighted
visual aids, specifying four escalating monitoring types (Type A through Type D), with Type D — individual-
lamp-out monitoring meeting AC 120-57 — required at airports operating SMGCS at Category III minima.

The monitoring "type" selected during design directly drives cost and wiring complexity — Type D individual-
lamp monitoring on a runway edge circuit is a materially bigger control-system scope than Type A basic status,
so the required type should be pinned down from the airport's category/SMGCS status before the ALCMS is
specified, not assumed.

Confirm which monitoring type the project actually requires (tied to CAT I/II/III operations and any SMGCS
plan) before comparing ALCMS vendor proposals — a Type A system priced against a Type D requirement is not a
like-for-like comparison, and existing ALCMS installations are not required to be retrofitted after a later
revision.

### FAA AC 150/5345-27F — Wind Cone Assemblies

L-806/L-807 wind cone equipment specification — companion to the Annex 14 wind indicator entry above

Sets manufacturing and photometric requirements for windsock assemblies (Size 1/Size 2, styles I-A/I-B) and
their L-806/L-807 supports; internally lighted cones must meet a defined luminance band and move freely at
wind speeds of 3 knots or more.

FAA AC 150/5345-27F, FAA Specification for Wind Cone Assemblies Revision F, 15 Dec 2021 — cancels 27E (26 Sep
2013)

Covers windsock size/style classification, support-pole load capacity (Type L-807 supports must withstand a
defined bending moment without damage), free-movement performance from 3 knots, and — for internally lighted
(Style I-B) cones — a luminance band measured across the sock surface at set intervals and angles.

ICAO Annex 14 sets out where a wind direction indicator is sited and what it must show a pilot; this AC is the
equipment-side companion that lets a specific windsock/support assembly be tested and shown to meet that
intent, in the same way IEC 61823 backs up the Annex 14 beacon entry above.

When reviewing a wind cone submittal, confirm the luminance test data covers the full sock surface at the
specified intervals and angles, not just a single-point reading, and check the support type against the
project's design wind-load requirements in AC 150/5300-13.

### FAA AC 150/5345-3G — L-821 Panels for the Control of Airport Lighting

Manual/electromechanical control panel — the simpler alternative to a full ALCMS

Covers the L-821 panel for remote control of runway/taxiway lighting circuits, specifying panel types
(conventional vs facsimile), mounting classes, and control styles/modes (summary — verify exact panel-layout
tables in the current edition).

FAA AC 150/5345-3G, Specification for L-821 Panels for the Control of Airport Lighting Cancels 150/5345-3F (28
Sep 2007); a draft 150/5345-3H circulated 22 Aug 2018 would change the Emergency Generator Control Switch from
mandatory to optional — confirm whether it has since been finalized

Sets manufacturing requirements for L-821 panels used to remotely control airport lighting and auxiliary
systems, covering two panel types (conventional, facsimile), mounting classes, styles and control modes, with
panel layout tied to the specific circuits (runway, taxiway, PAPI, etc.) being switched.

L-821 panels remain a valid, simpler alternative to a full L-890 ALCMS on smaller airports where individual
lamp-out monitoring isn't required — the choice between the two is a project decision on control/monitoring
needs, not a straightforward "newer supersedes older" case, since both remain current, actively supported
specifications.

For a small/GA airport project, weigh an L-821 panel against a full ALCMS on actual control and monitoring
requirements rather than defaulting to the ALCMS as the more modern-sounding choice, and confirm current
status of the "G" edition against FAA's AC index before specifying.

### FAA AC 150/5345-5B — L-847 Circuit Selector Switch

Switches a single CCR's output across one or more series lighting circuits

Covers the L-847 circuit selector switch used to switch a single CCR's output between one or more series
lighting circuits — common on PAPI, stop-bar and taxiway-centreline feeds, and as the changeover point to a
standby regulator.

FAA AC 150/5345-5B, Specifications for Airport Lighting Circuit Selector Switch Cancels 150/5345-5A (23 Mar
1982); a draft 150/5345-5C circulated 4 Sep 2018 for industry comment — confirm whether it has since been
finalized

Specifies four types, two classes and two sizes of L-847 circuit selector switch for switching a CCR's series-
circuit output, including an optional monitoring contact-closure feature and door-interlock switch, qualified
through a high-voltage switching-cycle test under rated load per the current revision.

A circuit selector switch lets one CCR serve more than one series loop (e.g. switching between a PAPI circuit
and a stop-bar circuit) without a dedicated regulator per loop, or lets a standby regulator be brought online
across several circuits — it sits functionally between the CCR and the loop, not inside either.

When a single CCR is specified to feed multiple independent circuits, or a standby-regulator arrangement is
shown on the SLD, confirm an L-847-qualified selector switch of the correct load rating is in the BOQ — a
common omission is sizing the CCR correctly but leaving the switching device off the schedule entirely.

## AGL Specifications, Test Standards, AAI Requirements & IS 12290

Which document sets the specification for runway, taxiway, approach and PAPI lighting, which test standards
apply, and how AAI and IS 12290 fit in. Summaries only; verify against the controlling document.

System | Governing documents on this page | What the specification should state

Runway lighting specification | ICAO Annex 14, Ch. 5 (spacing, colour) · DGCA CAR Section 4 · FAA AC 150/5345-46F (fixtures) | Light types, spacing, colour and colour-transition points, fixture standard and the project documents that govern each

Taxiway lighting specification | ICAO Annex 14 taxiway edge and centre line entries · FAA AC 150/5345-46F (fixtures) | Edge and centre line layout, fixture standard, circuit arrangement and the tests to be witnessed

Approach lighting specification | ICAO Annex 14 approach lighting entry · FAA AC 150/5345-51 (flashers) · FAA AC 150/5340-30J (installation details) | Approach category, pattern and fixture types, flasher equipment, installation details and acceptance checks

PAPI technical specification | ICAO Annex 14, Ch. 5 and Doc 9157 Part 4 (siting) · FAA AC 150/5345-28H (L-880/L-881) | Siting and glide-path angle basis, unit type, aiming and commissioning checks, and fail-to-night-mode behaviour on photocell loss

### Runway Lighting Specification & Runway Lighting FAA

A runway lighting specification should state the light types, spacing, colour and colour-transition points,
the fixture standard and the project documents that govern each. It draws on ICAO Annex 14 Ch. 5 and DGCA CAR
Section 4; runway lighting FAA references normally point to FAA AC 150/5345-46F for the fixtures.

### Taxiway Lighting Specification

A taxiway lighting specification should state the edge and centre line layout, the fixture standard, the
circuit arrangement and the tests to be witnessed. It draws on the ICAO Annex 14 taxiway edge and centre line
entries and FAA AC 150/5345-46F for fixtures.

### Approach Lighting Specification

An approach lighting specification should state the approach category, pattern and fixture types, the flasher
equipment, installation details and acceptance checks. It draws on the ICAO Annex 14 approach lighting entry,
FAA AC 150/5345-51 for flashers and FAA AC 150/5340-30J for installation details.

### PAPI Technical Specification & PAPI FAA

A PAPI technical specification should state the siting and glide-path angle basis, the unit type, aiming and
commissioning checks, and the fail-to-night-mode behaviour on photocell loss. It draws on ICAO Annex 14 Ch. 5
and Doc 9157 Part 4 for siting; PAPI FAA references normally point to FAA AC 150/5345-28H (L-880/L-881) for
the equipment.

Component | Key standard | Critical test

Airport lighting test standards (equipment) | FAA AC 150/5345-53D · FAA AC 150/5345-46F | Equipment certification and fixture requirements, as the project specification calls for them

Runway light test standards | ICAO Annex 14, Ch. 5 · DGCA CAR Section 4 | Spacing and colour-transition check against the approved layout

Taxiway light test standards | ICAO Annex 14 taxiway entries · FAA AC 150/5345-46F | Layout, spacing and fixture checks, plus circuit tests on the series circuit

PAPI test standards | FAA AC 150/5345-28H · ICAO Annex 14 and Doc 9157 Part 4 | Fail-to-night-mode on photocell loss, and re-verification of the siting calculation if the approach area changes

In-service series circuit | IEC 61821:2011 | Periodic insulation and loop resistance

Isolating transformer | IS 12290:1987 · FAA AC 150/5345-47C | Insulation resistance and 20-cycle endurance test

### Runway Light Test Standards

Runway light test standards come from ICAO Annex 14 Ch. 5 and DGCA CAR Section 4. The critical check is
spacing and colour-transition against the approved layout.

### Taxiway Light Test Standards

Taxiway light test standards come from the ICAO Annex 14 taxiway entries and FAA AC 150/5345-46F. Check
layout, spacing and fixtures, plus circuit tests on the series circuit.

### PAPI Test Standards

PAPI test standards come from FAA AC 150/5345-28H and ICAO Annex 14 with Doc 9157 Part 4. The critical checks
are fail-to-night-mode on photocell loss, and re-verification of the siting calculation if the approach area
changes.

### AAI AGL Specification, AAI PAPI Specification & AAI Airport Lighting Standards

An AAI specification is a project specification (Level 5 in the standards hierarchy above). It sits beneath
DGCA CAR requirements, ICAO Annex 14 and the equipment standards, and it decides which of them govern a given
tender. For an AAI AGL specification or an AAI PAPI specification, read the tender document itself, then check
each referenced standard for its edition and any amendments. Where AAI airport lighting standards and a
summary on this page differ, the controlling requirement prevails. See also Airfield Ground Lighting in India
.

### IS 12290 Airport Lighting & IS 12290 Isolating Transformer

IS 12290:1987 is the Bureau of Indian Standards specification for isolating transformers for airport lighting
systems. It covers construction, ratings and testing, including insulation resistance and a 20-cycle endurance
test, and it was prepared with reference to FAA AC 150/5345-47. When reviewing an IS 12290 isolating
transformer test certificate, confirm it reports the 20-cycle result and both primary and secondary insulation
resistance, because a single hi-pot pass/fail is incomplete against this standard. Confirm exact figures
against your copy of the standard.

## Aerodrome Lighting Standards, Requirements & Testing

### Airport lighting design standards

Airport lighting design standards set what the lighting system must provide and how it is arranged: which
lights are needed, their layout, colours, intensity levels and power supply. Design starts from the
aerodrome's operating category and the standards its authority applies, then follows the project
specification.

### ICAO Annex 14 aerodrome lighting

ICAO Annex 14 aerodrome lighting requirements are the international baseline for runway, taxiway and approach
lighting, stop bars, PAPI and signs. They describe what visual aids must do, and States may adopt or adapt
them in their own rules. Always use the edition and amendments your authority has adopted.

### ICAO airfield lighting standards

ICAO airfield lighting standards are the Standards and Recommended Practices in Annex 14, supported by ICAO
design and maintenance manuals. They set the performance and arrangement of the lights, not the product
design, so equipment specifications come from other documents.

### FAA airfield lighting requirements

FAA airfield lighting requirements are set in advisory circulars on installation and maintenance and in
equipment specifications for fixtures, regulators, transformers and cables. They are more product-specific
than ICAO, and apply where a project or tender names them.

### DGCA India aerodrome lighting

DGCA India aerodrome lighting requirements come from the Civil Aviation Requirements for aerodromes, which
adopt ICAO provisions with national differences. Indian aerodrome projects should follow the current CARs
together with the airport operator's specification.

### BCAS airport lighting requirements

BCAS airport lighting requirements relate to lighting for airport security, such as perimeter and security
areas, rather than aviation visual aids. They are separate from DGCA and ICAO rules on AGL. Check the current
BCAS circulars for the airport concerned.

### Airport lighting inspection standards

Airport lighting inspection standards define what must be checked, how often and how defects are classified
and recorded. The aviation authority's rules and the airport's maintenance programme set the schedule, and the
manufacturer's instructions add detail.

### AGL testing standards

AGL testing standards cover electrical tests such as circuit resistance and insulation, photometric tests of
light output, and functional tests of control and monitoring. The test method, instruments and acceptance
criteria should be taken from the specified standard and approved test plan.

### Airport lighting specification standards

Airport lighting specification standards are the documents a project specification points to for equipment and
installation, such as equipment specifications and IEC standards. A specification should name each standard
with its edition, so bids can be compared.

### Airfield lighting standards comparison

An airfield lighting standards comparison shows how ICAO, FAA, IEC and Indian Standards differ in purpose and
detail: ICAO sets the operational requirement, FAA documents specify products and installation, and IEC and IS
cover equipment performance and safety. They are often used together on one project.

### ICAO vs FAA lighting requirements

ICAO vs FAA lighting requirements differ in structure and wording, and in some colours, intensities and
arrangements. Where a project mixes both, the specification must say which one governs each item, so the
installed system is consistent.

### Runway lighting testing

Runway lighting testing checks that edge, threshold, centreline and touchdown zone lights work correctly after
installation and during service. It includes circuit tests, brightness step checks and light output
measurements, using the methods in the applicable standard.

### Taxiway lighting testing

Taxiway lighting testing covers edge, centreline and stop bar lights: circuit and insulation tests, correct
colours and operation, and photometric checks where required. Results are recorded against the approved test
plan.

### Airfield lighting control system

The airfield lighting control system lets controllers switch circuits and set brightness, and reports the
status of regulators and circuits. Standards cover its functions, response and monitoring, and the system
should be tested together with the CCRs and the lights.

# AIRFIELD GROUND LIGHTING IN INDIA

India's rapidly developing airport infrastructure requires dependable Airfield Ground Lighting systems for
runways, taxiways, approach areas, visual guidance and associated airfield infrastructure — from major
international airports and CAT II/III facilities to regional airports, defence airfields and heliports.

Precision AGL Solutions provides application-focused AGL solutions covering equipment, components, technical
support, installation, testing, commissioning, photometry, maintenance and retrofit requirements for airport
and airfield projects across India.

## AGL Standards & Compliance in India

AGL projects in India should be developed against the requirements applicable to the particular aerodrome and
project. Indian airport tender and technical documentation can reference a combination of ICAO standards and
guidance, DGCA requirements, AAI / airport-specific specifications, BIS / Indian Standards, IEC standards, and
FAA specifications where specifically required by the project.

For example, an AAI tender for airfield ground lights references ICAO Annex 14 Volume I, ICAO Airport Design
Manual Parts 4 and 5, IEC TS 61827, FAA AC 150/5345-46F and FAA Engineering Brief 67D. It also refers to DGCA-
CAR compliance and relevant BIS requirements for acceptance testing of indigenous products.

IS 12290:1987 — isolating transformers for airport lighting systems. IS 12291:1987 — constant-current
regulators for airport lighting systems. IS 11071 — inset-type aerodrome lighting fittings. IS 12309 Parts 1 &
2 — installation and maintenance of aerodrome lighting fittings.

There is no single generic specification set that applies to every Indian AGL project. The applicable
requirements should always be checked against the airport, project tender, approved design, applicable DGCA
requirements, AAI or airport specifications and equipment-specific standards.

## ICAO vs FAA for AGL in India

ICAO provides international Standards and Recommended Practices for aerodromes, while FAA Advisory Circulars
provide U.S. specifications and guidance. For projects in India, the applicable specification depends on the
project documentation — and AAI tenders show both references can occur within the same procurement framework.

#### ICAO — commonly relevant for

- Aerodrome visual aids

- Runway and taxiway lighting

- Approach lighting

- Operational requirements

- Aerodrome design

#### FAA — may appear for specific equipment

- FAA AC 150/5345-46 for airfield lighting equipment

- FAA Engineering Brief 67D for LED lighting considerations

- Other FAA equipment specifications where referenced by the project

Practical approach: identify the project requirement → identify the applicable standard → check equipment
compliance → verify testing requirements → complete installation and commissioning.

## Runway & Taxiway Lighting for Indian Airports

Indian AIP publications show active use of different runway and approach lighting configurations, including
CAT I and CAT II/III applications, along with taxiway centreline lighting, stop bars and runway guard lighting
at aerodromes operating under low-visibility procedures. The complete system should be considered when
selecting or replacing individual components.

## LED Airfield Lighting in India

LED technology is increasingly relevant to modern Indian airport lighting projects, applicable to runway edge,
threshold, runway end, taxiway, centreline, approach lights, airfield signs and other compatible visual aids.
AAI procurement documentation explicitly refers to both LED and non-LED airfield ground lights, with
FAA/ICAO/DGCA-CAR compliance requirements for applicable projects.

## AGL Installation & Maintenance in India

AGL installation requires coordination between lighting equipment, electrical infrastructure, civil works and
airfield operational requirements. Maintenance is essential for maintaining availability and supporting
airport operations, particularly for airports running low-visibility procedures.

#### Primary Circuit

Primary cable routing, primary connector installation, series-circuit connections, isolating transformer
installation.

#### Secondary Circuit

Secondary connector assembly, fixture connection, cable termination, equipment identification.

#### Lighting Equipment

Elevated fixtures, inset fixtures, runway lights, taxiway lights, approach lighting, sign systems.

#### Installation Quality

Correct positioning and orientation, cable/connector inspection, transformer installation, electrical testing,
fixture alignment, functional verification, final commissioning.

#### Maintenance Activities

Visual, fixture, connector and transformer inspection, series-circuit and cable testing, CCR checks, fault
diagnosis, component replacement, photometric testing, post-maintenance verification.

BIS lists IS 12309 Part 1 as the Indian code of practice for installation of aerodrome lighting fittings and
Part 2 for maintenance. For low-visibility operations, serviceability of critical AGL facilities becomes
particularly important — Indian AIP material documents specific AGL serviceability and inspection requirements
associated with LVP and CAT II/III operations.

## AGL for CAT II / CAT III Airports in India

CAT II and CAT III operations require specialised aerodrome facilities and carefully maintained visual aids.
Indian AIP material documents CAT II/III AGL installations, critical runway lighting circuits, stop bars,
taxiway centreline lighting and power-supply arrangements at Indian airports.

Power Supply & Availability — for critical AGL systems, the power architecture and changeover performance are
important parts of the overall installation. Hyderabad Airport — current AIP information describes UPS support
for critical AGL circuits and automatic DG takeover arrangements. Kolkata Airport — current AIP information
describes CAT II/III precision approach lighting and AGL power-supply requirements linked to DGCA CAR
requirements.

Maintenance & Serviceability — CAT II/III operations place greater importance on AGL serviceability. AIP
procedures for Indian aerodromes specify inspection and operational consequences associated with unserviceable
critical lighting facilities.

## PAPI in India: Requirements, Standards, Installation & Manufacturers

PAPI India projects supply a visual glide-path reference through PAPI (Precision Approach Path Indicator)

approach category are set by the aerodrome design and the applicable DGCA and ICAO provisions, so each project
should confirm them against its approved documentation.

### PAPI Airport India: PAPI Requirements India

Which runway ends need PAPI, and whether a full PAPI or a reduced system is used, follows the runway type,
approach and the approved aerodrome design.

- Runway-end selection and approach angle

- Unit count and spacing on the runway

### PAPI Standards India

## Airport, Runway & AGL Photometry in India

AGL photometry in India verifies that installed airfield lights deliver the intensity, beam pattern and colour
the specification requires. Airport photometry is used for new installations, acceptance, periodic checks and
before and after LED retrofit.

#### Runway photometry India

Runway photometry covers edge, threshold, end, centreline and touchdown-zone lights, measured against the
intensity and beam requirements that apply to each light type.

- Intensity and beam spread

- Aiming and alignment check

- Colour of emitted light

#### Airport photometry India

Airport photometry extends to taxiway, approach and PAPI lighting, so the whole visual-aid system can be
assessed rather than individual fixtures only.

- Taxiway centreline and edge lights

- Approach lighting

- PAPI beam and transition setting

#### AGL photometry India

AGL photometry results support acceptance decisions, maintenance planning and replacement of lights that no
longer meet their required output.

- Acceptance and commissioning records

- Periodic performance checks

- LED retrofit validation

Photometry complements electrical testing: a fixture can be energised and still fall short of its required
light output, which is why photometric measurement is commonly part of acceptance and periodic checks on
Indian airfields.

Scope, standards, equipment list, testing, commissioning, warranty and spares for airport lighting packages.

Compare tender requirements with the series circuit, CCR capacity and control interface of the existing or

#### Airport lighting tender specification India

#### Runway lighting tender & runway lighting BOQ

Edge, threshold, end, centreline and touchdown-zone lights with transformers, cable, connectors, bases and
testing.

#### Taxiway lighting BOQ, approach lighting BOQ & approach lighting tender

Taxiway edge and centreline lights, guidance signs and approach lighting items listed circuit by circuit.

Airport lighting specification India: a usable specification states the governing standard for each item, the
photometric and electrical acceptance criteria, installation tolerances, documentation to be submitted and the

which one governs each item.

## CCR, Isolating Transformer, Cable & Connectors for Airport Lighting in India

The series circuit is the backbone of an AGL installation. Choosing and matching the CCR, isolating
transformers, cable and connectors is central to every airport lighting project in India.

### CCR airport lighting India

The constant current regulator supplies the fixed series-circuit current and sets the light intensity steps.
CCR capacity must suit the circuit load.

- Constant current regulator India: IS 12291 and project specification

- Intensity steps and output current accuracy

- Control and monitoring interface

### Isolating transformer airport lighting India

Isolating transformers couple each light to the series circuit and keep the circuit working if a lamp or LED
fails.

- IS 12290 and project specification

- Ratings matched to fixture load

- Open-circuit protection behaviour

### Airport Lighting Cable India & Airport Lighting Connector India

Cable and connectors carry the series circuit through ducts and trenches, and their condition affects circuit
reliability and insulation resistance.

- Airport lighting cable India: rating and insulation

- Airport lighting connector India: moulded or kit-type

- Insulation-resistance testing after installation

### AGL Compliance Documentation in India | ICAO, DGCA, AAI, BIS

Canonical URL: https://rahulsharmaagl.in/agl-standards-compliance-india.html

**Page summary:** AGL compliance documentation in India: how ICAO, DGCA, AAI, BIS and project specifications combine, with the relevant Indian Standards for AGL equipment.

# AGL STANDARDS AND COMPLIANCE IN INDIA

AGL projects in India should be developed against the requirements applicable to the particular aerodrome and
project.

Indian airport tender and technical documentation can reference a combination of ICAO, DGCA, AAI, BIS, IEC
and, where specifically required, FAA frameworks.

## ICAO, DGCA, AAI, BIS & Project Specifications

AGL projects in India should be developed against the requirements applicable to the particular aerodrome and
project. Indian airport tender and technical documentation can reference a combination of several frameworks
at once.

## How These Frameworks Combine in Practice

An AAI tender for airfield ground lights references ICAO Annex 14 Volume I , ICAO Airport Design Manual Parts
4 and 5 , IEC TS 61827 , FAA AC 150/5345-46F and FAA Engineering Brief 67D . It also refers to DGCA-CAR
compliance and relevant BIS requirements for acceptance testing of indigenous products.

## DGCA Requirements & AAI / Airport Specifications

The Directorate General of Civil Aviation (DGCA) provides the Indian regulatory framework applicable to civil
aviation and aerodrome operations. Airport operators and implementing agencies layer their own project-
specific requirements on top of this.

#### DGCA & Civil Aviation Requirements

Depending on the project, applicable DGCA requirements and CARs may affect:

- Aerodrome visual aids

- Lighting facilities

- Low-visibility operations

- CAT II/III facilities

- Inspection and serviceability

- Operational availability, testing & maintenance

#### AAI / Airport-Specific Requirements

Airport operators and implementing agencies may issue their own:

- Technical specifications

- Approved equipment lists

- Tender specifications, drawings, design criteria

- Inspection & testing procedures, acceptance criteria

- Approved makes / equivalent requirements

## Relevant BIS Documentation

Standard | Scope

IS 12290:1987 | Isolating transformers for airport lighting systems

IS 12291:1987 | Constant-current regulators for airport lighting systems

IS 11071 | Inset-type aerodrome lighting fittings

IS 12309 Parts 1 & 2 | Installation and maintenance of aerodrome lighting fittings

The applicable edition, scope and project requirement should always be verified before using a standard as a
compliance basis.

## IEC Standards in AGL Projects

IEC standards and technical specifications may also form part of an Indian airport lighting project. AAI
tender documentation may, for example, reference IEC TS 61827 alongside ICAO, FAA and DGCA requirements.

IEC compliance should not automatically be assumed for every AGL component — the applicable IEC document
should be identified from the project specification and equipment scope.

## FAA Specifications in Indian AGL Projects

FAA specifications are U.S. documents, but they routinely appear in Indian airport tenders — for example FAA
AC 150/5345-46 or FAA Engineering Brief 67D. Their use depends entirely on the project documentation.

FAA reference in an Indian tender does not mean the project is governed exclusively by FAA requirements. The
complete project specification must always be reviewed.

## ICAO and FAA Serve Different Purposes

#### ICAO

International aerodrome Standards and Recommended Practices covering:

- Aerodrome design

- Runway & taxiway visual aids

- Approach lighting

- Operational requirements & aerodrome facilities

#### FAA

U.S.-based equipment specifications and engineering guidance, often specified for:

- Airfield lighting equipment & LED fixtures

- Equipment & photometric performance

- Electrical characteristics

- Specific product requirements

Do not ask only “ICAO or FAA?” Instead ask: which documents are specified by the project, and what requirement
does each document control? An Indian tender can legitimately contain references to both.

## A Five-Step Compliance Review

## Building a Project-Specific Compliance Matrix

A compliance matrix is one of the most useful documents during tendering, engineering and equipment approval.
It helps prevent the common mistake of assuming that compliance with one standard establishes complete project
compliance.

Requirement | Reference | Equipment / System | Compliance | Evidence

Aerodrome visual aid | ICAO Annex 14 | AGL system | To be verified | Design / calculation

Regulatory requirement | DGCA / CAR | Applicable system | To be verified | Compliance statement

Equipment requirement | Project specification | Equipment | Comply / Deviate | TDS

Indian Standard | Applicable IS | Equipment | Comply / N/A | Test certificate

FAA requirement | Applicable FAA document | Specified equipment | Comply / N/A | Type test / TDS

Installation requirement | IS 12309 / project spec | Installation | To be verified | Inspection

Acceptance test | Project specification | Equipment / system | To be verified | FAT / SAT report

## Mapping Standards to Individual Components

#### Constant Current Regulators

IS 12291:1987 plus project-specification review of:

- Output current steps & regulation performance

- Protection functions

- Monitoring & remote control interface

- Factory & site testing

#### Isolating Transformers

IS 12290:1987 plus project-specific checks on:

- Rating, primary & secondary voltage

- Insulation & thermal performance

- Waterproofing / environmental rating

- Type, routine & acceptance testing

#### Inset-Type Fixtures

IS 11071 plus application-specific review of:

- Photometric performance

- Mechanical & electrical characteristics

- Installation & environmental protection

- Project-specific FAA / ICAO requirements

## Installation and Maintenance Standards

#### Installation — IS 12309 Part 1

Covers primary/secondary cable and connector installation, transformer installation, fixture positioning and
orientation, equipment identification, earthing/bonding, electrical and functional testing, and final
commissioning.

#### Maintenance — IS 12309 Part 2

Covers visual and component inspection, series-circuit and CCR checks, fault diagnosis, photometric testing
and beam alignment verification. Serviceability becomes particularly critical for CAT II/III and low-
visibility operations.

## LED Retrofit Is a Whole-System Question

LED conversion is not simply a matter of replacing a conventional lamp with an LED fixture. An LED retrofit
should be evaluated as a complete series-circuit system.

## CAT II / CAT III Compliance

CAT II and CAT III operations introduce additional requirements for precision approach and low-visibility
operations, depending on the approved airport configuration.

The complete system must be considered: Lighting → Electrical Supply → CCR → Series Circuit → Control →
Monitoring → Backup Power → Maintenance → Operational Availability. Indian AIP material provides airport-
specific lighting configuration, power arrangement and serviceability information.
